Drops the commits through `throughSeq` and advances the floor; idempotent; beyond `lastSeq` is `invalid/args`.
Trims run one at a time, so the stored floor only rises and equals the one in memory.

symbols.name: ChordStore.commit
symbols.signature: commit(writes: readonly StagedWrite[], fence: CommitFence, context: Context): Promise<number>
symbols.comment:
Commits `writes` as one seq when the commit queue reaches it: `fence.admit()` at the entry of its step (its
group's), the writes in their order (retirements, creations, the rest), the outbox commit, `lastSeq` and the
allocator's value, `COMMIT`, then `fence.adopt` before the next step starts. Resolves with the seq. A refused
admission rejects `released`. A step the backend rolled back after the step's own code threw (a refusal, D4)
rejects with that error unchanged and the store goes on; any other failure (`BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, a
throwing `adopt` or metrics adapter) is an unknown outcome that stops the store (`storage_failed`). `context`
counts the step (no abort once queued).

Group commit: the commits queued while a step runs form one group, which the next turn admits and writes in one
backend transaction (each commit its own seq, outbox commit and adoption, in queue order; the metadata once), so a
busy store costs a transaction per group, not per commit. If one of them refuses, the group rolls back and its
commits run again one by one as above: the refusal stays its own commit's.

symbols.name: ChordStore.commitSeries
symbols.signature:
commitSeries(
		commits: readonly SeriesCommit[],
		receive: (index: number, seq: number, ids: readonly number[]) => void,
		context: Context,
	): Promise<SeriesResult>
symbols.comment:
Commits `commits` in one backend transaction when the commit queue reaches them, one seq each, in order: each
commit's `check`, which writes nothing, then its writes as `commit` writes them, with its own outbox commit and the
metadata (a commit without writes takes no seq: it stands at the one before). A `check` that throws refuses its
commit: the series stops there and the transaction commits the ones before it. A check whose backend statement
failed, and a throw of a commit's writes, roll the whole series back and reject with that error, the store going
on (D4); any other failure is an unknown outcome that stops the store, as for `commit`. After `COMMIT`,
`receive(index, seq, ids)` is called per stored commit, in order, before the next step starts (`ids`: its created
documents). Resolves with what it stored.
inputs: receive: (index: number, seq: number, ids: readonly number[]) => void

or closed; a backend error fails the store unless `context` was aborted (then `aborted`); a read settling after
the store stopped rejects `unavailable/storage_failed`. `read` returns data and never throws for a request: an
adapter checks a request from what it returned, after the guard (slice 6b §1.4).

symbols.name: ChordStore.#grouped

memory, the counts and each commit's adoption in order. When a commit's own writes throw (a refusal, D4), the
transaction rolls back whole and every commit runs again alone, admitted already: only the ones whose own writes
throw are refused, as without grouping. Any other failure is an unknown outcome that stops the store.

The store (slice 6a §2, §3, slice 6b §1): opened over a backend, one commit queue that serializes only the commit

step (the seal fence's admission check, `BEGIN`, the writes in their order, the outbox commit, `lastSeq` and the

allocator's value, `COMMIT`, then the owner's adoption), group commit (S18: the commits queued behind a running step

share the next step's backend transaction), the id allocator, the claims of its tables and documents, reads guarded

as Durable's `GuardedStorage` guards them, Durable's Storage semantics for a refused step (D4), and the stop after an

unknown outcome.

the newest version with its indexes (no replay); an older one is migrated eagerly, one version at a time, in its

those columns: the fingerprint names the version being reached, which resume, export and import check.

packages/chord/src/surfaces/client.ts.comment:
A client host with its plugins (slice 11 §2, §4, decisions "Slice 11, P4" to "P6"): what a page and a terminal's

sandbox both run. A client host (no address) loads the plugin scripts it started with beside the app's core facets,

keeps its link to the server with the connection loop, and holds the kind's scripts object: a new set fetches the

changed scripts and reloads the host in place (a failed plugin keeps its old facet; a failed fetch is tried again);

a new base bundle means this client's code is outdated, which the app answers by starting over (a page reloads). The

surface specifics (how a socket opens, how a script is fetched, what is outdated) are given.

symbols.name: RETRY_INITIAL_MS
symbols.comment:
The connection loop (slice 11 §2, decision "Slice 11, P6"; p2's `keepConnected`): a client keeps one link to the

server and replaces it when it ends. After a drop it reconnects after a growing pause (250 ms doubling to 5 s; a

connection that stayed open 10 s resets it), at once on a wake (visible again, back online, network changed); it

replaces an open socket silent past the server's ping interval on a wake, gives up a socket not open after 20 s, and

stops when the app's `canRetry` says no (an outdated client, a guest's ended share). The environment (time, timers,

wakes) is given, so the same loop runs in a page and in a terminal's sandbox.

The first retry pause after a failed or short-lived connection: 250 ms, doubling from there.

symbols.name: RETRY_MAX_MS
symbols.comment: The longest retry pause: 5 s (and the pause while offline).

symbols.name: STABLE_MS
symbols.comment: A connection that stayed open this long counted as working: the next retry starts at the initial pause again.

symbols.name: CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS
symbols.comment: A socket not open after this long is given up (browsers have no handshake timeout).

symbols.name: STALE_MS
symbols.comment: The server's heartbeat pings every 15 s: an open socket silent for longer than this is presumed dead on a wake.

symbols.name: WAKE_GRACE_MS
symbols.comment: After a wake, messages held while the client was frozen get this long to arrive before the socket is judged.

symbols.name: ConnectionState
symbols.comment: The connection as the app shows it: an attempt under way, open, or waiting for the next attempt.

symbols.name: SocketEvents
symbols.comment: What one socket reports to the loop.

symbols.name: SocketEvents.received
symbols.comment: Any frame: the server's pings keep an open socket from looking silent.

symbols.name: LoopLink
symbols.comment: One attempt's connection as the loop sees it: it closes once, and closing it ends it at once.

symbols.name: LoopEnvironment
symbols.comment: What the loop runs in: the clock, timers, whether the device is online, and its wake events.

symbols.name: LoopEnvironment.after
symbols.comment: Runs `callback` after `ms`; returns its cancel.

symbols.name: LoopEnvironment.online
symbols.comment: `false` when the device is known to be offline.

symbols.name: LoopEnvironment.onWake
symbols.comment: Calls `listener` when the client may have been away (visible again, online, network changed); returns its removal.

symbols.name: LoopOptions
symbols.comment: What the loop takes.

symbols.name: open
symbols.comment: Opens one socket and its link; the socket reports to `events`.

symbols.name: canRetry
symbols.comment: Asked after every close; `false` stops the loop. A rejection counts as `true` (unreachable, try again).

symbols.comment: Keeps a client connected until `stop`.

symbols.comment: Between a close and `canRetry`'s answer; a wake meanwhile retries at once.

symbols.name: Loop.connect
symbols.comment: Starts an attempt.

symbols.name: Loop.stop
symbols.comment: Stops the loop and closes the current link.

symbols.name: Loop.#closed
symbols.comment: `attempt`'s link closed: asks `canRetry`, then schedules the next attempt.

symbols.comment: Schedules the next attempt: at once (`now`), else after the backoff (offline: the longest pause).

symbols.name: Loop.#wake
symbols.comment: A wake: a pending retry runs now; an open socket silent too long is replaced once its overdue ping is checked.

that register themselves, a client host kept connected and current, a host's loaded plugins, themes, and messages and

packages/chord/src/surfaces/language.ts.comment:
A language and rendering in it (decision "Messages and languages in the app kit" (1), (3), refined in the build): a

`Language` is a locale with its text direction, the host's composed catalogs and where fallbacks are reported. A

render is synchronous, and while one runs its language is the current one: a message function's own `formatTime` or a

plain `t(...)` it calls renders in it. Outside a render there is no current language (a server, a test, a log line):

`t` renders the first catalog. No module-wide setting (the current language exists only while a render runs): one

process runs many hosts, and a server renders per recipient.

packages/chord/src/surfaces/messages.ts.comment:
Messages in code (decision "Messages and languages in the app kit" (1), (4), refined in the build): a plugin defines

its texts once, per namespace, in a shared `messages.ts` every facet that renders imports: `defineMessages("notes", {

en: {...}, de: {...} })` returns a typed `t`. The first catalog defines the keys and their argument types; every

other catalog must have the same keys with the same signatures (a missing key, an unknown one or a wrong argument is

a type error); values are strings or functions (plurals, word order). `t` renders in a language: bound to a host's

(`useMessages`, `scope.messages`, `t.in`), or plain, in the render under way's, else in the first catalog.

`t.message` builds a message as data (`{ namespace, key, params }`) for state, notices and errors, which each client

renders with `t.render` in its own language, checked at runtime (it crossed a link).

gzip-compressed JSON lines, one outbox commit (a batch) or one archive part (a snapshot) per line. gzip, because

`CompressionStream` offers it in Node, Workers, and browsers alike, and a browser viewer reads batches too.

symbols.name: UploadResult
uploadSession
symbols.comment:
Upload what this copy committed since it last shared the remote's history, from the store's outbox, and trim the
outbox through what the remote acknowledged. Every device continues a session as its own; whichever creates the slot
first continues the session, so an upload that is acknowledged stays.

A session the remote does not have yet, whose outbox does not reach back to its first commit (turned on later, or
trimmed, as for a copy renamed after it diverged), starts with an archive slot: the store's `export()` at its head.

A slot this device created already is an upload whose response was lost: the remote has the history up to its end,
and the upload goes on from there.

Apply a batch body to `store` as it streams, in chunks of about `APPLY_BYTES`, skipping the commits the store has
(a pull resuming inside a batch). Each chunk is one `applyBatch()` transaction; a pull stopped between chunks
resumes after the last applied one.

symbols.name: pullSession
symbols.comment:
Apply what the remote has after the local head; into an empty backend, that restores the session (from an archive
when the history starts with one) and opens its store with an outbox. Resolves with the store, which the caller
owns and closes. Nothing may hold the store's claims (no `StoreStorage`, no Harness): `applyBatch()` refuses then.

A copy with commits it has not uploaded rejects with `UnsyncedCommitsError` instead of getting the remote's commits
spliced onto its own. A copy whose history folding removed rejects with `HistoryUnavailableError` and restores into
a fresh backend.
symbols.output: Promise<{ readonly store: Store; readonly head: Seq }>

symbols.name: foldSession
symbols.comment:
Fold a session's history into one snapshot: restore it into `scratch` (an empty backend; a file or a Durable Object's
SQLite storage, not `:memory:`, so the restored store is not held in memory), upload its `export()` as a snapshot, drop the commits of the batches it covers, keeping their
slots taken, and delete older snapshots. The remote runs this, not clients.

symbols.name: FlushScheduler
symbols.comment:
Decides when to flush: some time after a commit, sooner after an urgent one, one flush at a time. Commits that arrive
during a flush keep their urgency and schedule the next one when it ends. A failed flush is retried with backoff
until one succeeds, so the last commits of a turn do not wait for the next commit.

symbols.comment: Flush now, after a flush underway, and stop scheduling. A failure rejects.

packages/chord/src/sync/client.ts.comment:
Session sync over a Chord store's outbox: upload the commits after the last sequence a copy shares with a remote

into a slot the remote creates once, pull a copy forward with `applyBatch`, restore from an archive, fold history

into snapshots, and decide when to upload. The remote and the host's sync state are interfaces (`remote.ts`).



Bounded memory: bodies are streams (`batch.ts`). An upload reads the outbox a page at a time and stops a batch at

`BATCH_BYTES`; a pull applies a batch in chunks of at most `APPLY_BYTES`; a snapshot is exported and imported as it

streams. Nothing holds a whole batch, snapshot or store, so a Durable Object's isolate (128 MB) can run it.

symbols.name: FileSystemSyncRemote
symbols.comment:
A remote store in a directory, laid out as the real remote is: per session, one slot per batch start, holding where
the batch ends and which device created it, and snapshots named by their end. As the real remote, it creates a slot
only where the history ends. Creating a slot is check-then-write,
without the atomicity of the real remote across processes: for development and tests, with one process writing.

```text
{root}/{session}/slots/{after}.json     { after, to, device, archive?, folded? }, written once
{root}/{session}/batches/{after}.batch  the commits (or an archive), until folded
{root}/{session}/snapshots/{to}.batch   a store archive
{root}/{session}/meta.json             the host's description, last write wins
```

`TuiScope` (slice 11 §4, decision "Slice 11, P9"; p2's `TuiScope`): a terminal component's Chord resources, the

counterpart of the React bindings for terminal UI libraries. It holds references, follows watchables and registries,

calls one `changed` callback (the app's redraw) on every change, and releases everything at `dispose`. Its page state

is the host's, shared by every scope (React's `usePageState`): a scope opened again after a plugin reload finds it.

Its messages render in the host's language, and a change of the locale or a translation redraws. A reader can show

an optimistic value while a call is pending (React's `useOptimistic`).

References wait and rebind by themselves (no retry loop, unlike p2's); no terminal library dependency.

symbols.name: WatchEnd
symbols.comment:
Terminal result of one watch, tagged by `kind`. A watch ends only for good; a failure its source recovers from is a
`failed` call (`WatchCall`), and the watch stays open.

- `stopped`: `stop()` was called.
- `aborted`: the context the watch was acquired with was aborted.
- `ended`: the source closed (its owner ended or closed).
- `listener_error`: the listener threw or rejected with `error`.
- `failed`: the source failed for good with `error`.

symbols.name: WatchCall
symbols.comment:
One call of a JSON watch's listener, and one frame a source hands its watch, tagged by `kind`:

- `value`: the newest value, the ops that turn the previous value into it, and whether the document the watch follows
  was retired since the previous value call. A retirement does not end the watch: `value` is then what the address
  shows after it (the source decides; a Durable document keeps the last value the watch was given, with no ops), and a
  document created there later arrives as `[["r", value]]`, possibly in the same call.
- `failed`: the source cannot compute its value now, with `error`; the watch stays open, and the next value arrives as
  `[["r", value]]`. `WatchHandle.value` keeps the last value.

Plain data: the frame's context is the listener's second argument, never part of the call.
symbols.output:
| { readonly kind: "value"; readonly value: T; readonly ops: readonly Op[]; readonly retired: boolean }
	| { readonly kind: "failed"; readonly error: unknown }

symbols.comment:
The lifecycle both handles share: serialized delivery and termination. A source feeds it and ends it explicitly;
termination drops every reference the watch holds into its source, so a stopped watch that is still referenced keeps
nothing but its last value alive. Subclasses keep what is pending, each call apart from its frame's context, so the
call a listener gets carries nothing but its data.

symbols.comment: Set by `endAfterDelivery()`: the source sends nothing more; the watch ends `ended` once it delivered the rest.

symbols.name: WatchLifecycle.#end
symbols.comment: Set once, by `#terminate()`.

symbols.signature: constructor(value: T, detach: () => void, report: (error: unknown) => void)

symbols.comment: End the watch `aborted` when `signal` aborts; installed once.

symbols.name: WatchLifecycle.abort
symbols.comment: End the watch `aborted`: its acquisition context was aborted.

symbols.name: WatchLifecycle.end
symbols.comment:
End the watch with `end` at once, dropping what is pending: the source closed (`ended`), or failed for good
(`failed`). A failure the source may recover from is a `failed` call instead (`fail()`).

symbols.name: WatchLifecycle.endAfterDelivery
symbols.comment:
The source sends nothing more after its last frames, such as a retirement: take no more frames, deliver what is
pending, then end `ended`, after the running call returns, if one runs. Until then the watch stays attached, so
`end()`, `stop()`, an abort, and a throwing listener still end it first; a watch never started keeps what is
pending until one of them or `start()`.

symbols.comment: Something became pending: deliver it once started, never inline.

symbols.name: WatchLifecycle.#drain
symbols.comment:
Deliver until nothing is pending; what arrives during a call is taken after it returns. A watch whose source ended
ends once it delivered the rest and its last call returned.

symbols.name: WatchLifecycle.#terminate

symbols.name: Watch
symbols.signature: export class Watch<T> extends WatchLifecycle<T, WatchCall<T>> implements WatchHandle<T> {
symbols.comment:
The watch handle of a JSON source. Frames that arrive before `start()` or while the listener runs wait in one
`PendingOps` queue; the next call gets the newest value, the folded ops of every frame since the previous call (or
`[["r", newest]]` after the queue overflowed), `retired` when any of them was a retirement, and the newest frame's
context. A frame delivered alone is passed on as the source made it. A failure (`fail()`) drops the pending frames and
waits as one `failed` call; a value after it replaces it, and the first value call after a failure is `[["r",
value]]`. `detach` unsubscribes it from its source on termination; `report` gets a listener's throw, which also ends
the watch.

symbols.name: Watch.#lone
symbols.comment:
The source's call while it is the only frame pending: the call passes it on, with no allocation. A second frame
drops it, so its ops stay only as long as `PendingOps` keeps them (folded, or dropped by an overflow).

symbols.name: Watch.#newestValue
symbols.comment: The newest frame's value and context, while a call is pending; the context also marks that one is.

symbols.name: Watch.#retired
symbols.comment: A pending frame was a retirement.

symbols.name: Watch.#failure
symbols.comment: The newest frame was a failure: the next call is this.

symbols.name: Watch.#replace
symbols.comment: A failure came after the last value call: the next value call replaces the root, and ops are not kept.

symbols.name: Watch.advance
symbols.comment:
Queue the frame `call`. A value's ops turn the previous value into it, and `retired` says the document the watch
follows was retired, which the next value call reports however many frames it folds; a failure is `fail()`.

symbols.name: Watch.fail
symbols.comment:
Queue a failure the source may recover from: the pending frames are dropped (`value` keeps the last delivered
value), the listener gets `{ kind: "failed", error }`, and the next value arrives as `[["r", value]]`.

symbols.name: Watch.#nextAfterFailure
symbols.comment: The pending failure, or the value after one as a root replacement (no ops were kept since the failure).

symbols.name: NativeWatch
symbols.signature: export class NativeWatch<T> extends WatchLifecycle<T, NativeWatchCall<T>> implements NativeWatchHandle<T> {
symbols.comment:
The watch handle of a native source: every value in order, one call each; past 100 pending values they collapse to
one, `replace()` or by default the newest value. A failure (`fail()`) drops the pending values and waits as one
`failed` call; a value after it replaces it. `detach` and `report` as for `Watch`.

symbols.name: NativeWatch.#pending
symbols.comment:
Pending values in order, each followed by its frame's context, from `#head` on. Values are kept raw: the call a
listener gets is built when it is taken, so a value an overflow drops costs no object. A read index instead of
`shift()` takes a backlog in constant time per value; taken slots are cleared at once, the array is emptied once
all of it was taken, and its taken prefix dropped after 100 values.

symbols.name: NativeWatch.#failure
symbols.comment: A pending failure and its frame's context; nothing else is pending meanwhile.

symbols.name: NativeWatch.constructor
symbols.signature: constructor(value: T, detach: () => void, report: (error: unknown) => void, replace?: () => T)

symbols.name: NativeWatch.advance
symbols.comment: Queue `value`, the source's new value; it replaces a pending failure.

symbols.name: NativeWatch.fail
symbols.comment:
Queue a failure the source may recover from: the pending values are dropped (`value` keeps the last delivered
value), and the listener gets `{ kind: "failed", error }`.

packages/chord/test/examples/17-limits-a.comment:
Size limits per part and compression at the origin. A host with a synchronous compressor (`nodeCompression` on

Node) deflates each JSON part above 16 KiB once, when it encodes it; relays forward it as it is; the end that owns it

inflates it, within its link's decoded limit. A browser has no synchronous deflate: it sends uncompressed and

inflates with `DecompressionStream`, later messages of its link waiting in order. Only a part that shrinks is sent

deflated, and never hold params. Clients never send compressed parts: a host sends its call arguments up its parent

link uncompressed, and a link the server accepted (a child) refuses compressed parts as a protocol error (a small

part could inflate to 64 MiB there). A part past a limit fails only its own hold or call (`too_large/part`); the

link stays. Limits and the threshold count UTF-8 bytes.

packages/chord/test/examples/30-host-roo.comment:
`host.root(fn, context)`: a call scope for code outside objects (a Durable tool, a CLI command). `fn` gets a ctx like a

method handler's: the host's principal (or one a trusted caller names), this host's incarnation, the context's

telemetry and signal, and `ctx.get` for references. When `fn` settles, or the context aborts, or the host closes, the

scope is sealed: its signal aborts, its references are released, and a late `ctx.get` is refused `released`; so code

that ignores its signal fails at its next use of Chord. The rule: await what you start in a root or a handler; a

change left running when the scope seals is cancelled, rejects and is reported (`transaction_cancelled`). (p3 wraps

it as `chord(fn, context)` for Durable's tools.)

the host-lifetime objects; requests made here and holds arriving on links wait only for that publication, never for

`load` resolves when each host-lifetime object had its first outcome: live, failed by its own cause, or parked with

no blocker here still without one (a wait on another host ends the first pass).

while a call runs on its old code, a search index with a native restarts after its running call drained, and a

removed plugin's object ends while its holder waits for it to come back.

packages/chord/test/examples/36-plugin-f.comment:
Plugin failures (slice 7c): every failure is per plugin. At startup a plugin whose setup throws is left out and the

others run (a consumer of what it would serve waits). At a reload a plugin whose new code fails keeps its old code and

is listed in the report's `failed`: a syntax error (its build failed), a module that throws while it is evaluated

(`mapStack` names the plugin's file and line), a factory that throws while the host stages it. The closure rule: a

provider and its consumer edited together, the provider broken, the consumer kept on its old code too (its new code

needs the provider's new version) and still working; the next good edit applies both. Last, a restart whose new code

needs an object that takes a while to open: the old code keeps serving until it is open.

packages/chord/test/examples/60-session-.comment:
Session sync as decided (decisions S3, S5, S7, W9, "The outbox is optional, internal and versioned", "p3 meeting,

2026-11-02"), played with Chord's real pieces: a laptop store with an outbox, `store.outbox.read`/`trim`,

`store.export` with `encodeJsonl`, `importStore`, and batch apply, `applyBatch` (internal: exported from

`chord` marked internal, imported here from `src/store/apply-batch.ts`; it takes the `ChordStore` behind

`openStore`'s `Store`). Radius and the laptop's sync client are stand-ins written for this example (`radius.ts`,

`sync.ts`), not Chord APIs: the sync layer is not built yet (slices.md, "The sync layer").

Steps: 1. a session on the laptop; 2. the handshake and a first upload; 3. a second sync moves only the tail;

4. a bootstrap from an archive for a session whose outbox was turned on late; 5. "continue on Radius" and the epoch

fence (the split), then the same without the fence (silent divergence); 6. back to the laptop with a pull.

Run from packages/chord:

node --conditions=source --experimental-strip-types test/examples/60-session-sync/main.ts

packages/chord/test/examples/60-session-.comment:
STAND-IN for Radius, not a Chord API: what example 60 needs of the server side of session sync, in memory. Per

session id it keeps a replica store (SQLite in memory, as a Durable Object's SQLite would be), the commit log (what

R2 would hold; the replica's outbox is moved into it and trimmed after every change), the driver and its epoch.

Batches and archives cross a "wire" as JSON and JSONL bytes, so the replica checks them as a trust boundary.

`checkEpochs = false` turns the epoch fence off, to show what the gap analysis warned about.

packages/chord/test/examples/60-session-.comment:
STAND-IN for the laptop's sync layer, not a Chord API: the decided handshake (ask Radius for `lastSeq`, send the

outbox from `lastSeq + 1`, trim through the answer), the bootstrap from an archive, the eager upload of new commits

after the last acknowledgement (S5), the split on an old epoch (S7) and the pull of Radius's commits. Built on

Chord's real pieces: `store.outbox.read`/`trim`, `store.export`, `encodeJsonl`, and `applyBatch` (internal).

symbols.name: telemetry
symbols.comment:
1. Start the app: the kit makes the data directory, the server's store and host, HTTP and the owner link. Nobody is

signed in yet, so the page answers 401. The owner opens the link: its page posts the token from the URL's fragment

and gets a session cookie.

symbols.name: OWNER
symbols.comment:
2. A list on its own worker. Code acting as the owner gets the groceries list's `Todos`: the request goes to the

list's address, and the first one starts its worker. The same call in a root of the server acts as the server.

symbols.name: token
symbols.comment:
3. Routes. A command-line client on this machine sends the owner token file as a bearer token; the route's

`ctx.get` acts as the request's principal, so the todo is the owner's.

symbols.name: html
symbols.comment:
4. The page: the app's template with the base bundle, the plugins' combined script and their stylesheets. A watch

starts at the current value; its listener gets only what changes after.

symbols.name: frames
symbols.comment:
5. The terminal client (Node 26.5.1 or later): the launcher signs in with the owner token file, downloads the

terminal's base bundle and the plugins' terminal scripts and runs them in its sandbox, here on a scripted terminal.

symbols.name: login
symbols.comment:
7. A second user. Ada picks a name (the kit's ephemeral login) and connects a client host of her own over the links

endpoint, as a page does. A host serves nothing before `load`: a client with nothing to load calls `load([])`.

symbols.name: ownerChooses
symbols.comment:
8. Languages. The owner chooses German: a preference the server keeps per principal, which every client of the owner

follows, so the terminal redraws in German without restarting. Ada's pick is her own. Clearing the done todos

leaves a notice as data, a key and its parameters: the server's plain render is the English catalog, the

terminal renders the same state in German.

symbols.name: BEFORE
symbols.comment:
9. An edit applied in place: the lists plugin's worker facet trims a todo's text, so a blank one is empty and the

store refuses it with Chord's `invalid/args`, which reaches Ada as it would a refused argument. The

watcher marks the plugin dirty; applying the changes rolls it out to the server, the list's worker, the page and

the terminal. On the worker each object of the plugin restarts: running calls finish on the old code, new calls

wait for the new code, documents and tables stay (the store's live query runs again on its new attempt). Ada's

reference stays live while the old code drains, then shows `loading` briefly and the new code's snapshot.

The edit: `add` in the `Todos` view, before and after.

symbols.name: archive
symbols.comment:
10. Export and import. The list's running worker writes its own store and files as one archive and goes on; importing

the archive makes a new list with the same todos. An address that has data is never overwritten.

The lists plugin's contract: a list's todos as one principal sees them, on the list's worker. Its facets of every

kind import it, and so do code and tests outside the plugin (they resolve `@todo/app/v1` as plugins do).

The lists plugin's messages, in English (the source of truth) and German: one file every facet that renders imports,

and the worker, which writes a notice as data for each viewer to render.

The lists plugin on the server: a JSON API for command-line clients. A route runs as whoever sent the request (the

kit answered 401 before this code runs when nobody signed in), so its `ctx.get` reaches the list's worker as them.

The lists plugin in the terminal: its title, the groceries list's todos, live, done ones muted, and the list's

notice. Its texts are in the terminal's language (`scope.messages`), and its catalogs are contributed here: the

plugin's own languages are its contributions to the terminal's `Translations`.

the owner "Clear done", and the list's notice. The list is the page's `#hash`, `groceries` without one. The

half-typed todo is page state: a reload of this plugin remounts the panel, and the page keeps what was typed. Its

texts are in the page's language (`useMessages`), and its catalogs are its contribution to the page's `Translations`.

The lists plugin's worker facet, tested alone with `testPlugin`: built as production builds it, evaluated with the

app's real API module and loaded on a host of its own (an in-memory store) at a list's address. Each test runs code

as a principal of its choice: a user gets the `member` variant, the owner `owner`; a todo keeps who added it, one

without text is refused, and clearing leaves a notice as data. The test imports the app's API by its package name and

the plugin's contract from its `contract.ts`, as the facets do.

packages/chord/test/examples/63-optimist.comment:
A call's answer follows its state (decision of 2026-11-05), and the optimistic value a terminal UI shows while a

call is pending (`TuiScope.optimistic`, React's `useOptimistic`). A session's worker renames its session and pushes

the new title to the server's index inside the method, as an app's worker should. A slow terminal client holds the

index (served by the server) and calls `rename` (relayed by the server to the worker). The server's window for the

client is full, so its index change waits; before the server forwards the worker's answer it sends that waiting

state, so when the call settles in the client the index already has the new title: the optimistic title is replaced

by the real one and the old one never shows again.

Run from packages/chord:

node --conditions=source --experimental-strip-types test/examples/63-optimistic-answers.ts

symbols.name: ProviderV2

symbols.comment: A dependent: it holds the provider, and `ping` calls the provider's `x` back.

symbols.comment: The plugin at `code`; `raised` serves `ProviderV2` (the dependent's code then needs it).

symbols.signature: async function workAcross(label: string, host: ReturnType<typeof createHost>, next: ReturnType<typeof plugin>)
symbols.comment: Starts `work`, reloads to `next` while it waits at its gate, then opens the gate: prints how `work` ended.

symbols.name: host
symbols.comment:
1. Both objects restart while the provider's `work` runs. Its `ctx.get` of the dependent reaches the dependent's new

attempt, which binds the provider's open old attempt; the back-call `x` is old work too, so it runs on the

provider's old code. No call waits for the drain it is part of.

symbols.name: Fresh
symbols.comment:
3. Old work that would wait for its own drain: `work` creates an object whose new code needs the raised provider,

whose new attempt waits for `work` to end. It fails at once with `unavailable/reload_cycle`, naming the chain,

instead of waiting for the reload drain bound.

With params: an object of no params is a host-lifetime one, opened at the load.

symbols.name: bounded
symbols.comment:
4. A call still running at `reloadDrainTimeout` (default 5 s, at most `closeTimeout`) is cut `released`: long work

belongs in jobs. Here the bound is 200 ms and `work` never opens its gate.

packages/chord/test/examples/64-old-work.comment:
Old work finishes on old code (decision "Reload restarts every affected object; old work finishes on old code"). A

reload restarts every live object of a changed plugin. The calls running at the commit, and every call they cause

(found through the `ctx` they pass on, and over trusted links), are old work: they run on the old attempts, which

stay open until that work drained and their successors' requests are ready. New calls wait for the new code. Here:

a provider's running call reaches its dependent while both restart, once with the provider's contract raised; a wait

that would cycle through its own drain fails at once; and a call still running at `reloadDrainTimeout` is cut.

Run from packages/chord:

node --conditions=source --experimental-strip-types test/examples/64-old-work.ts

packages/chord/test/examples/65-files.ts.comment:
Files (decision "Files v2"): the app kit's file storage, one `Files` object per host, its bytes in the host's

`files/` and its index in the host's store. Every file lives in a space at a path; folders are index entries and a

move changes only the index; bytes never change (a write to a path adds a version, a copy shares the bytes); a key

makes a retried write store nothing; versions are found by path, folder, `ref` and `key`; `FilesFolder` lists one

folder live; each space has a summary an app mirrors to its server; `copyFiles` copies a host's files to a new host.

`startServer` and `startWorker` load `filesFacet` on their hosts; an app with hosts of its own loads it itself, as

here.

Modules that only exist when cloudflare.ts is built by Wrangler. Consumers get the real

declarations from @cloudflare/workers-types or `wrangler types`; these keep this repository's

type check free of a Workers type dependency and are not published.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxDurableObject
symbols.signature: export class CodemodeSandboxDurableObject<Env = unknown> extends DurableObject<Env> {
symbols.comment:
The remote end of `RemoteCodemodeSandbox`: a Durable Object whose one RPC method runs a script's
VM and calls back into the client for every tool call.

Deploy it as its own Worker and bind it from the Worker that runs your agent with `script_name`.
A separate Worker is what keeps scripts off the agent's thread: a class in the same Worker can
share an isolate, and therefore a thread, with the objects that call it.

The object keeps no state between executions and never touches storage. Executions that reach
the same instance share its thread: they interleave while they wait on tools, and a script that
computes delays the others. Name instances per session (`getByName(sessionId)`) to keep one
session's scripts together, or per execution for full independence.

Limits apply to every request, whatever the client asks for. Override the fields in a subclass:

    export class CodemodeSandbox extends CodemodeSandboxDurableObject {
      protected maxInterruptBudget = 200_000;
    }

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxDurableObject.maxInterruptBudget
symbols.comment: Interrupt polls per execution; the client may only ask for less. See `InlineCodemodeSandboxOptions`.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxDurableObject.maxMemoryLimitBytes
symbols.comment: VM memory per execution; the client may only ask for less.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxDurableObject.execute
symbols.comment: Called by `RemoteCodemodeSandbox` over RPC. Resolves when the script has settled or was stopped.

packages/codemode/src/cloudflare.ts.comment:
Cloudflare Workers entry, for Workers built with Wrangler.

Wrangler's default `CompiledWasm` rule turns the `.wasm` import below into a
`WebAssembly.Module`; Workers cannot compile WebAssembly from bytes at runtime. Other bundlers
do not support the import: use `@earendil-works/pi-codemode/portable` with your own module there.

Two ways to run codemode on Cloudflare:
- `RemoteCodemodeSandbox` with a {@link CodemodeSandboxDurableObject} deployed as its own
  Worker: scripts run in a separate isolate and never block the caller. Use this from a Durable
  Object that serves a session.
- {@link createInlineCodemodeSandbox}: scripts run on the caller's thread. Simplest; a script
  that computes blocks the caller until it awaits a tool or uses up its interrupt budget.

symbols.name: MAX_REF_EXPANSIONS

symbols.name: LINE_TERMINATORS
symbols.comment: Characters that end a `//` comment.

symbols.name: renderDeclarations
symbols.comment:
Render TypeScript declarations for the script-visible API. Tools become members of
`declare const tools`, globals become `declare function` statements, and `ns.member` globals
members of `declare const ns`. Descriptions become doc comments; schemas become types.

name as the identifier scripts use. Input types longer than `inputMaxChars` render as `unknown`.

A tool's sample: the description followed by the tool's declaration. Used for tool
listings and `ALL_TOOLS` entries.

symbols.name: renderToolOutputType
symbols.signature: export function renderToolOutputType(schema: CodemodeJsonSchema | undefined): string
symbols.comment: The type a tool call resolves to: the output schema's type, and `unknown` without a schema.

symbols.name: renderGlobal
symbols.signature: function renderGlobal(head: string, global: CodemodeTool, indent: string): string

symbols.name: docComment

symbols.name: schemaToType
symbols.signature: export function schemaToType(schema: CodemodeJsonSchema, options: { maxChars?: number } = {}): string
symbols.comment:
Convert a JSON Schema to a TypeScript type expression: objects on one line (`{ a: string; b?: number; }`) with properties sorted by name,
or one property per line with `//` comments when a property has a description or constraints the
type cannot express (`// @integer @minimum 1 @default 20`); `Array<T>` for arrays. Local references
(`#/$defs/...`, `#/definitions/...`) resolve against `schema`; recursive and remote references
render as `unknown`. A result longer than `maxChars` is rendered again without the constraint tags,
and renders as `unknown` if it is still too long.

symbols.name: SchemaContext.resolving
symbols.comment: References being expanded on the current path, to stop at recursive types.

symbols.name: SchemaContext.tags
symbols.comment: Whether property comments include constraint tags.

symbols.name: resolveSchemaRef
symbols.signature: export function resolveSchemaRef(ref: string, root: unknown): CodemodeJsonSchema | undefined
symbols.comment:
The subschema a local `$ref` (`#`, `#/$defs/Item`) names in `root`, or undefined for remote references and
references that name nothing. Pointer segments are URI-decoded and JSON Pointer unescaped (`~1` is `/`, `~0` is `~`).

symbols.name: constraintTags
symbols.comment:

packages/codemode/src/portable.ts.comment:
Sandboxes that need no Node built-ins: `InlineCodemodeSandbox` runs the VM on the calling thread
and `RemoteCodemodeSandbox` runs it in another isolate. Neither imports `node:*` modules, so this
entry works in Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, and browsers. `CodemodeSandbox`, which uses
worker threads, stays in the main entry.

symbols.name: VmEvents.failure

symbols.name: VmChannel
symbols.comment: The host's handle on a running VM.

symbols.name: VmChannel.stop
symbols.comment: Requests VM shutdown. Called once; may resolve before a worker or remote VM actually exits.

symbols.comment:
`code` is an async function body: `return` and top-level `await` work.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxBase.start
symbols.comment:
Run `code` deterministically, with the caller answering its calls: the same script, start time, seed, tools,
globals, and store, answered with the same results in the same `seq` order, makes the same calls with the same
arguments and produces the same output, on any VM with the same fingerprint. A host can therefore replay it
after a restart. The VM runs in UTC, its clock reads `startedAt` and then the `now` of the result being
processed, its randomness comes from `seed`, and `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` do not exist.

The sandbox's own tools and globals are not used: the run declares its own, and every call goes to
`options.onCall`. Never rejects for script failures; abort through `options.signal` to end the run with an
error the script cannot catch.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxBase.close
symbols.comment: Aborts in-flight executions (they resolve with `kind: "aborted"`) and rejects new ones.

packages/codemode/src/runtime/execution..comment:
Host side of an execution, shared by every place a VM can run.

The host owns everything the script must not influence: the tool table, call records, output,
the deadline, the caller's abort signal, and the decoding of what the VM reports. The VM itself
runs somewhere a {@link VmLauncher} decides: a worker thread (`CodemodeSandbox`), the calling
thread (`InlineCodemodeSandbox`), or another isolate reached over RPC (`RemoteCodemodeSandbox`).
The two sides only exchange the messages in `protocol.ts`, so the launchers differ in transport
and termination, not in behavior.

Lifecycle of one execution:
1. The constructor arms the deadline and abort listener, then asks the launcher for a channel.
2. Messages from the VM arrive through {@link VmEvents.message}; tool calls run here and their
   results go back through {@link VmChannel.post}. Replies produced before the launcher has
   returned its channel are queued and flushed when it arrives.
3. The first terminal event wins: `done`, `crash`, a launcher failure, the deadline, or an abort.
   `finish()` aborts pending tool calls, asks the channel to stop, and resolves the result once
   that request completes. A worker or remote VM may exit later. Later events are ignored.

The launcher, not this class, is responsible for actually stopping a running VM: a worker is
terminated, an in-thread VM is interrupted and disposed, and a remote VM is told to stop at its
next exchange.

symbols.name: workerLauncher
symbols.comment:
Each execution gets its own worker thread and QuickJS VM. A fresh worker per run keeps
termination simple: a runaway script, including one that only spins the microtask queue, is
killed with `terminate()` and cannot poison a later run. Before terminating, the host sets a
shared interrupt flag that the VM polls, because Bun's `terminate()` cannot stop a thread that
is spinning in wasm. Stopping requests termination without waiting for exit: some built-ins do
not poll the flag, so on Bun a worker can outlive the script's result.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandbox
symbols.comment:
Runs JavaScript in a QuickJS VM (a separate wasm instance) inside a worker thread. The worker
keeps script execution off the host thread: QuickJS runs synchronously, so a spinning script on
the host thread would block its event loop. Requires `node:worker_threads` (Node or Bun); see
`InlineCodemodeSandbox` and `RemoteCodemodeSandbox` in `@earendil-works/pi-codemode/portable`
for other runtimes.

symbols.name: INLINE_MAX_STACK_SIZE
symbols.comment: Allows recursion about 1,000 calls deep and trips well before a 1 MB host stack overflows.

symbols.name: InlineCodemodeSandboxOptions.wasm
symbols.comment:
Compiled `quickjs-wasi/quickjs.wasm`. On Cloudflare, import it with Wrangler's `CompiledWasm`
rule (`@earendil-works/pi-codemode/cloudflare` does this); on Node, `loadQuickJSWasm()`.

symbols.name: InlineCodemodeSandboxOptions.interruptBudget
symbols.comment:
Interrupt polls an execution may use before it fails with `kind: "timeout"`. The only limit on
a script that computes without awaiting a tool. Default: {@link DEFAULT_INTERRUPT_BUDGET}.

symbols.name: inlineLauncher
InlineCodemodeSandbox
symbols.comment:
Runs each execution's QuickJS VM on the calling thread. Works in any runtime with WebAssembly
and microtasks; needs no worker threads, files, or Node built-ins. A script that computes
blocks the caller's thread until it awaits a tool or uses up its interrupt budget, so prefer
`CodemodeSandbox` where worker threads exist, and `RemoteCodemodeSandbox` to keep scripts off a
thread that must stay responsive (such as a Durable Object that serves a session).

packages/codemode/src/runtime/inline.ts.comment:
Runs the VM on the calling thread, for runtimes without worker threads (Cloudflare Workers and
Durable Objects, browsers) and for the server side of `RemoteCodemodeSandbox`.

Problem: QuickJS runs synchronously. While a script computes, the host's event loop does not
run, so neither the deadline timer nor an abort signal can fire. On Workers even `Date.now()` is
frozen during synchronous execution, so the VM cannot check a clock either. Example: with a
worker thread, `while (true) {}` is stopped by the host's 200 ms timer; on the calling thread
that timer never gets a chance to run.

Solution: an interrupt budget. QuickJS polls its interrupt handler periodically while a script
runs; this launcher counts the polls across the whole execution and interrupts the script once
the count passes the budget. The execution then fails with `kind: "timeout"`. The deadline and
abort signal still work whenever the script waits on a tool, since the event loop runs then.

The rate of polls depends on the code and the machine. Measured with a tight loop: about 50,000
per second of CPU on an Apple M-series laptop and about 10,000 per second on Cloudflare Durable
Objects (October 2026). The default of 100,000 allows roughly 2 to 10 seconds of uninterrupted
computation; keep it well below the platform's own CPU limit, because hitting that limit resets
a Durable Object instead of failing one script.

Once the VM reports `done` or `crash`, the result is decided, so the VM is interrupted at the
next poll instead of running on until the host stops it. Example: a script that keeps printing in
a `for (;;)` loop after its output limit was reached would otherwise run until the budget ran out
and be reported as a timeout.

Stack: the VM runs on the caller's stack, which is smaller than a worker thread's (about 1 MB
on Node's main thread), so QuickJS's stack guard is set to {@link INLINE_MAX_STACK_SIZE}.

Reentrancy: VM callbacks run inside QuickJS. Messages from the VM are delivered to the host in
a microtask, after the VM has returned, so host code (tool calls, `finish()`, disposal) never
runs inside a VM callback and never re-enters the VM.

symbols.name: MAX_STORE_VALUE_CHARS
symbols.comment:
JavaScript evaluated inside the QuickJS VM before the script runs.

The VM is its own wasm instance, so nothing here guards a realm boundary.
The prelude keeps the host bridge in a closure so the script cannot call it
directly, and builds `tools`, `ALL_TOOLS`, the output helpers (`text`, `image`,
`exit`, `console`), and globals on top of it. Tool arguments and results cross
as JSON strings and are parsed on this side.

Output helpers: `text(value)` appends a text item (non-strings are
JSON-stringified), `image(urlOrItem)` appends an image from a base64 `data:` URL, an
`{ image_url }` object, or an image block `{ type: "image", data, mimeType }`, and `exit()` ends the script
successfully. `console.*` appends text items marked as console output.

`store(key, value)` and `load(key)` are synchronous: they work on a snapshot of
JSON text passed in as `storeJson`, and the keys the script wrote are reported
with a successful "done".

Evaluates to a function `(bridge, toolsJson, globalsJson, storeJson) => { settle, run, stalled }`.
`settle(id, ok, payload, propertiesJson)` settles call `id`; a rejection's `Error` gets the own properties of the
`propertiesJson` object, except `name`, `message`, and `stack`.
`toolsJson` lists `{ name, jsName, description }`: `tools[jsName]` and `tools[name]` call the
tool, and `ALL_TOOLS` lists `{ name: jsName, description }`.
`stalled()` reports a script that has not finished while no host call is pending: with no timers
or I/O in the VM, nothing can ever resume it.
`globalsJson` lists `{ name, spread }`; `a.b` names are grouped into a frozen `a` object.
`bridge(kind, a, b, c)` with kind "call" or "global" (id, name, argsJson),
"output" ("text" or "console", text) or ("image", data, mimeType), or "done" (ok, valueJsonOrErrorJson, writesJson).

Before anything else the prelude freezes the built-ins and makes the built-in globals read-only.
The prelude shares them with the script, so a script that patched one (for example
`Array.prototype.toJSON`) could otherwise corrupt what the prelude reports to the host.

symbols.name: MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS
symbols.comment:

base64 image data, and items. The host keeps all output until the script ends, so without a
limit a script that prints in a loop grows the host's memory until it crashes. The item limit
covers loops that print empty strings.

packages/codemode/src/runtime/remote.ts.comment:
Runs the VM in another isolate, reached over an RPC boundary such as a Cloudflare Durable Object
stub, while tools keep running in the caller.

Problem: a VM on the calling thread blocks that thread while the script computes. In a Durable
Object that serves an agent session, a CPU-heavy script would stall every other request to the
session (including the user's abort) for seconds. Measured on Cloudflare (October 2026), a
script that computed for 10 seconds delayed the session's other requests by 10 seconds when it
ran in the session object or in a Dynamic Worker, but by about 50 ms when it ran in a Durable
Object of a separately deployed Worker.

Solution: the caller keeps the host role (`RemoteCodemodeSandbox`: tools, call records,
deadline, abort) and the remote side only runs the VM (`serveCodemodeRemote`, behind
`CodemodeSandboxDurableObject` in `@earendil-works/pi-codemode/cloudflare`).

Protocol, one RPC call per execution:

    client                                     remote
    remote.execute(request, exchange) ───────▶ starts the VM (in-thread, with interrupt budget)
                                     ◀─────── exchange([...outputs, call])   one call per tool call
    runs the tool, replies with result ──────▶ VM continues
                                     ◀─────── exchange([...outputs, done])   terminal, reply ignored
    execute() resolves ◀────────────────────── VM disposed

`exchange` is a function the client passes in; over Workers RPC it becomes a stub that calls back
into the client. Output is buffered on the remote side and sent with the next call or the
terminal message, so a script that prints in a loop does not make one RPC per line. Each
`exchange` carries at most one call, so concurrent tool calls are concurrent RPCs. Calls on one
stub are delivered in order, which keeps output ordered before the call or result that follows.

Termination: the client cannot interrupt a remote VM that is computing. When the client finishes
first (deadline, abort, `close()`), it answers every pending and later `exchange` with
`{ type: "stop" }`, and the remote stops the VM at that point. A script that computes without
calling a tool runs until its interrupt budget is used up. The remote reports that as a
`failure` message, which the client turns into the same `kind: "timeout"` error an in-thread
VM produces.

Failure: if the RPC call rejects (the remote isolate crashed, hit its CPU limit, or was
redeployed) or returns without a terminal message, the execution fails with `kind: "sandbox"`.

(512 KiB), which fits the 4 MB stack of a Node worker thread but not a 1 MB main thread.

packages/codemode/src/runtime/vm.ts.comment:
Drives one QuickJS VM through one script, independent of the transport that connects it to the
host. The worker thread, the in-thread launcher, and the remote server all run the VM through
this module, so the bridge between prelude and host exists once.

Contract with the caller:
- `post` receives every message for the host, synchronously from inside VM callbacks. The
  caller must not re-enter the VM from `post` (no `deliver`, no `dispose`); a worker posts to
  another thread, and the in-thread launcher defers delivery to a microtask.
- `deliver` hands the VM a tool result and runs the script until it waits again. It must only be
  called while the VM is idle, which holds for any caller that never re-enters from `post`.
- `shouldInterrupt` is polled by QuickJS while the script runs, and here between batches of
  promise jobs. Returning true throws an uncatchable error in the script; the VM then reports
  `crash` or a failed `done`. The job batches matter for a script such as `while (true) await
  null`: every iteration is a separate job that executes only a few opcodes, so QuickJS's own
  polling, which counts opcodes, would let it run for a long time between polls.
- The VM never decides on its own when it is finished: after `done` or `crash` it stays alive
  until the caller disposes it (or terminates the worker that hosts it).

Failures after the VM exists are reported as a `crash` message; `startVm` only rejects when the
VM cannot be created at all.

Deterministic mode (`data.deterministic`, used by `CodemodeSandboxBase.start()`): a script must make the same
calls with the same arguments every time it runs with the same results, so a host can replay it after a restart.
The VM is otherwise deterministic, because it only runs when the host delivers something and has no timers.
What remains is fixed here:
- Time: every WASI clock reads virtual time, `startedAt` and then the `now` of the result being processed, never going backwards.
  While the context is created, the realtime clock reads a value derived from the seed instead, because QuickJS
  seeds `Math.random()` from the first clock read, and which read comes first is the engine's business.
- Randomness: `random_get` draws from a PRNG over the seed.
- Timezone: UTC, not the host's.
- Garbage collection: `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` are not available; collection timing is not.
- Delivery order: results carry a `seq` and are applied strictly in that order, buffering early ones, because a
  transport (RPC replies) may deliver them in another order than the host sent them.
The VM reports `started` with its fingerprint before the script runs, and `idle` with the number of calls issued
after each drain, so the host can check a replay step by step.

packages/codemode/src/runtime/worker.ts.comment:
Worker thread entry. One worker runs one script inside a fresh QuickJS VM
(a separate wasm instance), relays tool calls and output to the host, and
reports the result. The host terminates the worker when the script settles,
times out, or is aborted; the worker exists so that a spinning script never
blocks the host thread.

Importing this module starts the worker. Hosts that bundle their code (for
example a Bun compiled executable) add a file that imports
`@earendil-works/pi-codemode/worker` as a separate entrypoint and pass its URL
or embedded-module string specifier as `workerUrl`.

MAX_TIMEOUT_MS
symbols.comment: Largest delay `setTimeout` supports, which bounds `timeout_ms`.

options line; the options JSON and the code are checked by {@link parseCodemodeSource}.

symbols.comment:
Aborted when the script finishes (including unawaited calls), the

symbols.name: CodemodeJsonSchema
symbols.signature: export type CodemodeJsonSchema = { [key: string]: unknown } | boolean;
symbols.comment: A JSON Schema document. Only used to render declarations; values are not validated against it.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.name
symbols.comment:
The script calls tools as `tools.<id>(args)`, where `<id>` is the name with characters that
are not valid in identifiers replaced by `_` (see `toCodemodeIdentifier`), and also as
`tools["<name>"](args)`. Globals are called as `<name>(args)` and must be identifiers, or
`<namespace>.<member>`, which groups them into a frozen namespace object.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.description
symbols.comment: Shown as a doc comment in {@link renderDeclarations}, and listed in `ALL_TOOLS` for tools.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.inputSchema
symbols.comment: Schema of the single argument. Rendered as the parameter type; `unknown` when omitted.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.outputSchema
symbols.comment: Schema of the resolved value. Rendered as the promise type; `unknown` when omitted.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.spread
symbols.comment: Globals only: `execute` receives all call arguments as an array instead of the first one.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.signature
symbols.comment:
Globals only: TypeScript parameter list and return type for {@link renderDeclarations}, for
example `(type: string, id?: string): Promise<Model[]>`. Replaces the rendering from the schemas.

symbols.name: CodemodeTool.execute
symbols.signature: execute(args: unknown, context: CodemodeToolContext): Promise<unknown> | unknown;
symbols.comment:
`args` is whatever the script passed, after a JSON round trip. The return
value must be JSON-serializable; a thrown error surfaces in the script as
an `Error` with the same message.

symbols.name: CodemodeOutputItem
symbols.comment:
One item of the script's output, in the order the script produced it: `text()` and `console.*`
produce text items, with `console: true` for `console.*`, and `image()` image items. `data` is base64.
symbols.output:
| { type: "text"; text: string; console?: true }
	| { type: "image"; data: string; mimeType: string }

symbols.name: CodemodeErrorKind
symbols.output:
| "script"
	/**
	 * The overall deadline expired, or a VM on the calling thread used up its interrupt budget.
	 * The execution ended and the VM was asked to stop; a worker or remote VM may still be computing.
	 */
	| "timeout"
	/** The caller's signal fired or the sandbox was closed. The execution ended and the VM was asked to stop. */
	| "aborted"
	/**
	 * The VM or its transport failed outside the script's control (for example a wasm trap, a missing
	 * worker file, or a remote sandbox that failed).
	 */
	| "sandbox"

symbols.name: CodemodeStoreWrites
symbols.comment: Keys the script changed with `store()`. Only successful executions report writes.

symbols.name: CodemodeStoreWrites.delete
symbols.comment: Keys stored as `undefined`.

symbols.name: CodemodeResult
symbols.comment:
`output` is kept for failed executions too, up to the failure. `exit()` completes with `value: undefined`.
`during`: in a {@link CodemodeSandboxBase.start} run that the script itself ended (it returned, threw, or exited),
the result being processed when it did.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxBaseOptions
symbols.comment: Options every sandbox accepts, wherever its VM runs.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxBaseOptions.globals
symbols.comment:
Functions exposed as top-level identifiers instead of on `tools`, for host helpers such as
attaching an image to the result. They behave like tools (JSON round trip, promise result)
but are not recorded in `result.calls`. Names must be identifiers and may not shadow the
built-in globals (`tools`, `ALL_TOOLS`, `console`, `text`, `image`, `exit`, `store`, `load`).

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxBaseOptions.timeoutMs
symbols.comment:
Overall deadline per execution, including time spent in tools. `Infinity` disables the
deadline; the execution then only ends when the script settles or is aborted.
Default: 300000.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxBaseOptions.memoryLimitBytes
symbols.comment:
Maximum memory the QuickJS VM may allocate. Allocations beyond it fail inside the script as
`InternalError: out of memory`. Default: no limit beyond wasm32's 4 GiB address space.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxOptions
symbols.comment: Options of `CodemodeSandbox`, which runs each VM in a Node or Bun worker thread.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxOptions.wasm
symbols.comment:
Compiled `quickjs-wasi/quickjs.wasm`, usually from {@link loadQuickJSWasm}. Default:
`loadQuickJSWasm()`, the file in the installed `quickjs-wasi` package. Pass it when that file
is not on disk, for example in a Bun compiled executable.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxOptions.workerUrl
symbols.comment:
Worker entry that imports `@earendil-works/pi-codemode/worker`. Default: this package's own
worker file. Pass it when this package is bundled, since the default is resolved relative to
the module that creates the sandbox. Bun compiled executables require the relative string
specifier of an embedded build entrypoint; other hosts usually use a URL.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxOptions.acquireWorker
symbols.comment:
Synchronously reserves capacity immediately before creating each worker, after loading wasm.
Throw to deny admission without starting a worker. Return a release callback, called once if
worker construction fails or when the worker actually exits, not when the result settles.
The release callback must not throw. Reservations can be shared across sandbox instances.

symbols.name: CodemodeSandboxOptions.onWorkerStarted
symbols.comment:
Called once for each worker started by execute() or start(). `exited` resolves when that worker
actually exits, which may be after the result and close() settle: on Bun a non-interruptible
built-in can delay termination. Use it to keep the worker counted against host concurrency
limits until it exits. A thrown callback error fails the execution and requests worker termination.

symbols.name: CodemodeHostCall
symbols.comment: A call the script made in a {@link CodemodeSandboxBase.start} run, answered with `CodemodeRun.deliver()`.

symbols.name: CodemodeHostCall.id
symbols.comment: The VM's own number for the call, `1`, `2`, ... in the order the script made its calls (tools and globals).

symbols.name: CodemodeHostCall.args
symbols.comment: What the script passed, after a JSON round trip; for spread globals the argument list.

symbols.name: CodemodeDeclaredTool
symbols.comment: A tool as a {@link CodemodeSandboxBase.start} run's script sees it: `tools.<name>` and its `ALL_TOOLS` entry.

symbols.name: CodemodeDeclaredTool.jsName
symbols.comment:
The identifier the script uses, `tools.<jsName>`. Default: `toCodemodeIdentifier(name)`. A host that replays a run
passes the one the run started with, so a changed mapping cannot rename a tool under a resumed script.

symbols.name: CodemodeDeclaredGlobal
symbols.comment: A global as a {@link CodemodeSandboxBase.start} run's script sees it; the same names as `globals` allow.

symbols.name: CodemodeOutcome
symbols.comment:
A call's answer. A rejection becomes an `Error` with `message` in the script, carrying the own properties of
`properties` (JSON values; `name`, `message`, and `stack` are ignored), for example `{ structuredOutput }`.
symbols.output:
| { ok: true; value: unknown }
	| { ok: false; message: string; properties?: Record<string, unknown> }

symbols.name: CodemodeDuring
symbols.comment: In a {@link CodemodeSandboxBase.start} run: the result the VM was processing when the script finished, 0 for its first run, and the calls issued by then.

symbols.name: CodemodeRunOptions.startedAt
symbols.comment: The VM clock's start, in ms since the epoch: `Date.now()` until the first result arrives.

symbols.name: CodemodeRunOptions.seed
symbols.comment: Seeds `Math.random()` and the VM's other randomness. A 32-bit unsigned integer.

symbols.name: CodemodeRunOptions.timeoutMs
symbols.comment: Deadline of this run in ms. Default: none (not the sandbox's default).

symbols.name: CodemodeRunOptions.onStarted
symbols.comment: The VM's fingerprint, before the script runs and before any of its calls.

symbols.name: CodemodeRunOptions.onCall
symbols.comment: The script made a call. Answer it with `CodemodeRun.deliver()`, now or later.

symbols.name: CodemodeRunOptions.onIdle
symbols.comment:
The VM processed result `seq` (`0`: the script's first run, before any result) and waits again, having issued
`issued` calls in total.

symbols.name: CodemodeRun
symbols.comment: A running {@link CodemodeSandboxBase.start} execution.

symbols.name: CodemodeRun.finished
symbols.comment:
Whether the run has its outcome: the script ended, timed out, or failed, or the run was aborted. Set when that is
decided, before `result` settles; calls can no longer be answered. It does not mean the VM has exited.

symbols.name: CodemodeRun.deliver
symbols.signature: deliver(seq: number, now: number, id: number, outcome: CodemodeOutcome): void;
symbols.comment:
Answer call `id` as result number `seq`. Results are numbered 1, 2, ... without gaps, and the VM applies them
strictly in that order, whatever order they arrive in: after a gap it waits for the missing number. While it
processes this one, its clock reads `now` (ms since the epoch), or the previous value if `now` is earlier.
Throws for a call that is not waiting for an answer, a `seq` used before, or a `now` that is not finite.

symbols.name: CodemodeExecuteOptions.timeoutMs
symbols.comment: Overrides the sandbox default for this execution.

symbols.name: CodemodeExecuteOptions.store
symbols.comment:
Values the script reads with `load(key)`. Must be JSON-serializable. The script's own
`store()` calls come back as `result.storeWrites`; persisting them is up to the caller.

symbols.name: CodemodeWasmModule
symbols.comment:
A compiled `WebAssembly.Module` of `quickjs-wasi/quickjs.wasm`. Typed opaquely because the Node
type definitions do not declare the WebAssembly globals (they live in the DOM lib).

symbols.name: loadQuickJSWasm
symbols.comment:
Read and compile the QuickJS wasm once per path. `path` defaults to the file in the installed
`quickjs-wasi` package; pass it when that file lives elsewhere, for example embedded in a Bun
compiled executable. A failed load is retried on the next call.

packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Built-in Tool Renderer Example - Custom rendering for built-in tools

Demonstrates how to override the rendering of built-in tools (read, bash,
edit, write) without changing their behavior. Each tool is re-registered
with the same name, delegating execution to the original implementation
while providing compact custom renderCall/renderResult functions.

This is useful for users who prefer more concise tool output, or who want
to highlight specific information (e.g., showing only the diff stats for
edit, or just the exit code for bash).

How it works:
- registerTool() with the same name as a built-in replaces it entirely
- We create the original definitions via createReadToolDefinition(), etc.
  and override only their renderers
- renderCall() controls what's shown when the tool is invoked
- renderResult() controls what's shown after execution completes
- renderShell: "self" lets a tool render its own outer shell instead of
  using the default boxed shell from ToolExecutionComponent
- The `expanded` flag in renderResult indicates whether the user has
  toggled the tool output open (via ctrl+e or clicking)

Usage:
  pi -e ./built-in-tool-renderer.ts

packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Claude Rules Extension

Scans the project's .claude/rules/ folder for rule files and lists them
in the system prompt. The agent can then use the read tool to load
specific rules when needed.

Best practices for .claude/rules/:
- Keep rules focused: Each file should cover one topic (e.g., testing.md, api-design.md)
- Use descriptive filenames: The filename should indicate what the rules cover
- Use conditional rules sparingly: Only add paths frontmatter when rules truly apply to specific file types
- Organize with subdirectories: Group related rules (e.g., frontend/, backend/)

Usage:
1. Copy this file to ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ or your project's .pi/extensions/
2. Create .claude/rules/ folder in your project root
3. Add .md files with your rules

Commands Extension

Demonstrates the pi.getCommands() API by providing a /commands command
that lists all available slash commands in the current session.

Usage:
1. Copy this file to ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ or your project's .pi/extensions/
2. Use /commands to see available commands
3. Use /commands extensions to filter by source

Confirm Destructive Actions Extension

Prompts for confirmation before destructive session actions (clear, switch, branch).
Demonstrates how to cancel session events using the before_* events.

Custom Compaction Extension

Replaces the default compaction behavior with a full summary of the entire context.
Instead of keeping the last 20k tokens of conversation turns, this extension:
1. Summarizes ALL messages (messagesToSummarize + turnPrefixMessages)
2. Discards all old turns completely, keeping only the summary

This example also demonstrates using a different model (Gemini Flash) for summarization,
which can be cheaper/faster than the main conversation model.

Usage:
  pi --extension examples/extensions/custom-compaction.ts

Custom Footer Extension - demonstrates ctx.ui.setFooter()

footerData exposes data not otherwise accessible:
- getGitBranch(): current git branch
- getExtensionStatuses(): texts from ctx.ui.setStatus()

Token stats come from ctx.sessionManager/ctx.model (already accessible).

directory is mounted at /workspace in the guest. File changes under
/workspace write through to the host; other guest filesystem changes are
isolated to the VM.

Setup:
  cd packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/gondolin
  npm install --ignore-scripts

Usage:
  cd /path/to/project
  pi -e /path/to/pi/packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/gondolin

Requirements:
  - Node.js >= 23.6.0 for @earendil-works/gondolin
  - QEMU installed (for example, `brew install qemu` on macOS)

Handoff extension - transfer context to a new focused session

Instead of compacting (which is lossy), handoff extracts what matters
for your next task and creates a new session with a generated prompt.

Usage:
  /handoff now implement this for teams as well
  /handoff execute phase one of the plan
  /handoff check other places that need this fix

The generated prompt appears as a draft in the editor for review/editing.

Inline Bash Extension - expands inline bash commands in user prompts.

Start pi with this extension:
  pi -e ./examples/extensions/inline-bash.ts

Then type prompts with inline bash:
  What's in !{pwd}?
  The current branch is !{git branch --show-current} and status: !{git status --short}

The !{command} patterns are executed and replaced with their output before
the prompt is sent to the agent.

Note: Regular !command syntax (whole-line bash) is preserved and works as before.

Streaming-Aware Input Gate

Demonstrates `event.streamingBehavior` to skip expensive pre-processing
during mid-stream steering, where low latency matters.

This extension prepends `git diff --stat` output when the user mentions

Start pi with this extension:

packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Jev router - a virtual model that plans on a strong model and implements on a cheap one.

Registers `jev/auto`, which routes between three OpenAI Codex models:

- Planning: GPT-5.6 Sol for complex work, GPT-5.6 Terra otherwise. The Jev classifier rates the
  first user message; planning stays on the chosen model.
- Implementation: GPT-5.6 Luna.

The planning model explores, plans, and makes the first edit. After the first successful `edit`
or `write` tool call, the next request of the same turn goes to Luna, and the session stays
there. A session therefore switches models once and accepts a single prompt-cache miss.

The phase is router state: Pi stores it on the session branch, so it follows the session tree
and survives compaction. The selected thinking level passes through as the reasoning effort of
the chosen model. Requests outside the agent loop, such as compaction summaries, go to Luna.

Requires TypeSafe credentials (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and an OpenAI Codex login.
Usage: pi -e ./jev-router.ts --model jev/auto

packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Preset Extension

Allows defining named presets that configure model, thinking level, tools,
and system prompt instructions. Presets are defined in JSON config files
and can be activated via CLI flag, /preset command, or Ctrl+Shift+U to cycle.

Config files (merged, project takes precedence):
- ~/.pi/agent/presets.json (global)
- <cwd>/.pi/presets.json (project-local)

Example presets.json:
```json
{
  "plan": {
    "provider": "openai-codex",
    "model": "gpt-5.2-codex",
    "thinkingLevel": "high",
    "tools": ["read", "grep", "find", "ls"],
    "instructions": "You are in PLANNING MODE. Your job is to deeply understand the problem and create a detailed implementation plan.\n\nRules:\n- DO NOT make any changes. You cannot edit or write files.\n- Read files IN FULL (no offset/limit) to get complete context. Partial reads miss critical details.\n- Explore thoroughly: grep for related code, find similar patterns, understand the architecture.\n- Ask clarifying questions if requirements are ambiguous. Do not assume.\n- Identify risks, edge cases, and dependencies before proposing solutions.\n\nOutput:\n- Create a structured plan with numbered steps.\n- For each step: what to change, why, and potential risks.\n- List files that will be modified.\n- Note any tests that should be added or updated.\n\nWhen done, ask the user if they want you to:\n1. Write the plan to a markdown file (e.g., PLAN.md)\n2. Create a GitHub issue with the plan\n3. Proceed to implementation (they should switch to 'implement' preset)"
  },
  "implement": {
    "provider": "anthropic",
    "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5",
    "thinkingLevel": "high",
    "tools": ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"],
    "instructions": "You are in IMPLEMENTATION MODE. Your job is to make focused, correct changes.\n\nRules:\n- Keep scope tight. Do exactly what was asked, no more.\n- Read files before editing to understand current state.\n- Make surgical edits. Prefer edit over write for existing files.\n- Explain your reasoning briefly before each change.\n- Run tests or type checks after changes if the project has them (npm test, npm run check, etc.).\n- If you encounter unexpected complexity, STOP and explain the issue rather than hacking around it.\n\nIf no plan exists:\n- Ask clarifying questions before starting.\n- Propose what you'll do and get confirmation for non-trivial changes.\n\nAfter completing changes:\n- Summarize what was done.\n- Note any follow-up work or tests that should be added."
  }
}
```

Usage:
- `pi --preset plan` - start with plan preset
- `/preset` - show selector to switch presets mid-session
- `/preset implement` - switch to implement preset directly
- `Ctrl+Shift+U` - cycle through presets

CLI flags always override preset values.

Raw agent frontmatter. Values are `unknown` because `parseFrontmatter` runs a
real YAML parser, so any scalar or collection can appear here.

A type alias rather than an interface: `parseFrontmatter` constrains its
parameter to `Record<string, unknown>`, and only an alias picks up the
implicit index signature that satisfies it.

symbols.name: parseToolList
symbols.comment:
Normalize a frontmatter `tools` value to a list of tool names.

Both spellings are valid YAML and both are in use:

    tools: read, bash        # string
    tools: [read, bash]      # array

so accept either. Anything else (a number, a map, a nested list) yields no
tools rather than throwing: this runs inside agent discovery, where a single
bad file must not take down every other agent in the same directory.

packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Tic-Tac-Toe extension - demonstrates executionMode: "sequential" on tools.

The user plays via /tic-tac-toe (arrow keys + Enter).
The agent plays via a single tool `tic_tac_toe` that takes ONE atomic action
per call. To play at (r, c) from its cursor (r0, c0) the agent must emit the
required move_* and a final `play` as SEPARATE tool_use blocks inside ONE
assistant response.

Move actions share the agent cursor and have a 300ms delay. Under the
default parallel tool-execution mode this races: `play` can resolve before
the earlier `move_*` calls finish and O lands on the wrong cell. With
`executionMode: "sequential"` the runner serializes the sibling calls and O
lands on the intended cell.

The user cursor (TUI-only) and the agent cursor (tool-only) are stored in
separate variables. Only the agent cursor is ever exposed to the agent.

packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Tool Override Example - Demonstrates overriding built-in tools

Extensions can register tools with the same name as built-in tools to replace them.
This is useful for:
- Adding logging or auditing to tool calls
- Implementing access control or sandboxing
- Routing tool calls to remote systems (e.g., pi-ssh-remote)
- Modifying tool behavior for specific workflows

This example overrides the `read` tool to:
1. Log all file access to a log file
2. Block access to sensitive paths (e.g., .env files)
3. Delegate to the original read implementation for allowed files

Since no custom renderCall/renderResult are provided, the built-in renderer
is used automatically (syntax highlighting, line numbers, truncation warnings).

Usage:
  pi -e ./tool-override.ts
