packages/coding-agent/examples/extension.comment:
Truncated Tool Example - Demonstrates proper output truncation for custom tools

Custom tools MUST truncate their output to avoid overwhelming the LLM context.
The built-in limit is 50KB (~10k tokens) and 2000 lines, whichever is hit first.

This example shows how to:
1. Use the built-in truncation utilities
2. Write full output to a temp file when truncated
3. Inform the LLM where to find the complete output
4. Custom rendering of tool calls and results

The `rg` tool here wraps ripgrep with proper truncation. Compare this to the
built-in `grep` tool in src/core/tools/grep.ts for a more complete implementation.

Sets a custom working message and indicator on session start so you can
verify they survive across loader recreations (e.g. between agent turns).

loader appears, not revert to the default gray "Working...".

packages/coding-agent/examples/sdk/14-co.comment:
Codemode, Tool Search, and MCP

The CLI loads `codemode`, `tool_search`, and MCP as built-in extensions. SDK sessions add
them to the resource loader's extension factories.

`codemode` and `tool_search` are registered inactive. Enable them through the `defaultTools` setting
(`tools` would also restrict the session to the named tools, which hides MCP tools), or let the
MCP extension activate them: `codemode` for servers with `codemode` exposure, `tool_search` for
servers with `deferred` exposure.

from `messages`), or undefined when the prompt is unchanged. Tool changes are declared by
the agent loop before the request.

A forced prompt does not affect the transcript: the structured sections are still diffed
and persisted, and the forced text is projected onto the request by
{@link _installAgentForcedPromptProjection}.

symbols.name: AgentSession._installHiddenDeclarationsProjection
symbols.comment:
Send a forced prompt as the provider's leading system prompt without recording it.

A `before_agent_start` handler that returns `systemPrompt` needs that exact text at the
head of the request; a mid-conversation system message would leave the original prompt
in place. The forced text is a rendering of the current prompt, so the transcript keeps
its structured sections and the request is projected instead: the system messages
collapse into one head holding the forced text and the current tools. Runs after the
`context` extension handlers.

Remove the declarations that `prepareLoadout` hooks hide from every request. The whole
transcript is filtered with the current set, so the projected declarations stay consistent
across requests and only change when the loadout does.

Manually compact the session context.

This is the manual entry point used by `/compact`, RPC, and extensions. It is
separate from automatic threshold/overflow compaction, which enters through
`_checkCompaction()` and `_runAutoCompaction()`. After preparation and the
`session_before_compact` hook, both paths call the lower-level `compact()`
function imported from `./compaction/index.ts`, unless the hook cancels or
supplies a custom result.

Aborts the current agent operation first. Manual compaction never retries or

symbols.name: AgentSession._checkCompaction
symbols.signature: private async _checkCompaction(assistantMessage: AssistantMessage, skipAbortedCheck = true): Promise<boolean>
symbols.comment:
Dispatch automatic compaction after `agent_end` or before prompt submission.
Manual compaction does not call this method; it enters through `compact()`.

Automatic cases:
1. Overflow with retry: a context-overflow error or recoverable length stop;
   remove the failed assistant message, compact, and retry the turn once.
2. Overflow without retry: a successful response exceeded the configured
   context window; compact but preserve the completed response.
3. Threshold without retry: valid or estimated context usage crossed the
   configured threshold; compact without retrying the completed response.

Each case calls `_runAutoCompaction()`. After preparation and the
`session_before_compact` hook, that method calls the lower-level `compact()`
function imported from `./compaction/index.ts`, unless the hook cancels or
supplies a custom result.

@param assistantMessage The assistant message to check
@param skipAbortedCheck If false, include aborted messages (for pre-prompt check). Default: true
@returns Whether the post-run loop should call `agent.continue()` for overflow recovery or queued messages

packages/coding-agent/src/core/agent-ses.comment:
AgentSession - Core abstraction for agent lifecycle and session management.

This class is shared between all run modes (interactive, print, rpc).
It encapsulates:
- Agent state access
- Event subscription with automatic session persistence
- Model and thinking level management
- Compaction (manual and auto)
- Bash execution
- Session switching and branching

Modes use this class and add their own I/O layer on top.

(antivirus, indexer, another pi checking the lock) still has it open. mkdir then fails with

EPERM until that handle closes. Retry this briefly so real permission errors still fail fast.

symbols.name: findCutPoint
symbols.comment:
Find the cut point in session entries that keeps approximately `keepRecentTokens`.

Algorithm: Walk backwards from newest, accumulating estimated message sizes.
Stop when we've accumulated >= keepRecentTokens. Cut at that point.

Can cut at user OR assistant messages (never tool results). When cutting at an
assistant message with tool calls, its tool results come after and will be kept.

Returns CutPointResult with:
- firstKeptEntryIndex: the entry index to start keeping from
- turnStartIndex: if cutting mid-turn, the user message that started that turn
- isSplitTurn: whether we're cutting in the middle of a turn

Only considers entries between `startIndex` and `endIndex` (exclusive).

symbols.name: serializeConversation
symbols.comment:
Serialize LLM messages to text for summarization.
This prevents the model from treating it as a conversation to continue.
Call convertToLlm() first to handle custom message types.

Tool results are truncated to keep the summarization request within
reasonable token budgets. Full content is not needed for summarization.

Thinking is omitted. Providers return summaries of the real reasoning, and
replayed thinking is often not part of the model's live context: for example,
a block that does not match its request is dropped. Including it can make the
summarization request larger than the context it summarizes. Visible text,
tool calls, and tool results record what happened.

symbols.name: ToolExposure
symbols.comment:
How the model reaches a tool. "Callable" means callable from other tools through
`ctx.executeTool()`, as the `codemode` tool does.

- `direct`: declared to the model while active, and callable while active.
- `model-only`: declared to the model while active, never callable. Use it for orchestrating or
  interactive tools.
- `codemode`: callable whenever registered. Not declared to the model unless explicitly
  activated. Codemode tools list it in their description.
- `deferred`: like `codemode`, but codemode tools do not list it; tool search can find it.
- `hidden`: registered but unreachable. Activating it has no effect.

`direct` and `model-only` tools are activated when they are registered; the others are not.
The active tool set (`getActiveTools`/`setActiveTools`) is the set declared to the model.

Agent Events

Fired before each LLM call. Can modify messages.

symbols.comment:
Type guard for narrowing ToolCallEvent by tool name.

Built-in tools narrow automatically (no type params needed):
```ts
if (isToolCallEventType("bash", event)) {
  event.input.command;  // string
}
```

Custom tools require explicit type parameters:
```ts
if (isToolCallEventType<"my_tool", MyToolInput>("my_tool", event)) {
  event.input.action;  // typed
}
```

Note: Direct narrowing via `event.toolName === "bash"` doesn't work because
CustomToolCallEvent.toolName is `string` which overlaps with all literals.

Unregister a previously registered provider.

Removes all models belonging to the named provider and restores any

symbols.name: ExtensionAPI.registerMcpServer
symbols.comment:
=========================================================================

MCP Servers

=========================================================================

Register an MCP server for this session, with the same config as an `mcpServers` entry in
`mcp.json`. The server connects next to the configured servers: on `session_start` when
registered during extension load, right away when registered later. Registering a name again
replaces the extension's earlier registration.

The registration is not saved; register again on every load. A server of the same name in
`mcp.json` takes precedence. Throws for invalid configs and for names another extension
registered. When no loaded extension handles MCP servers (for example because another MCP
extension replaced the built-in one), the registration is reported as an extension error.

@example
pi.registerMcpServer("jira", { url: "https://mcp.example.com/jira" });

symbols.comment:
Leave this extension out when another extension registers a tool, command, or flag with a
name it registers during loading, instead of reporting a conflict. The CLI's built-in MCP,
codemode, and tool search extensions use it, so for example an MCP extension that registers
`/mcp` replaces the built-in MCP support. The factory still runs, so it should only register

symbols.name: builtin
symbols.comment:
Supply the code of the `builtin:<name>` extension instead of loading as an inline extension.
`builtin:<name>` is an extension resource like a file: it loads by default, `pi config` lists
it, `-builtin:<name>` in the `extensions` setting and `--no-extensions` disable it, and
`-e builtin:<name>` loads it explicitly. It is hidden from the startup Extensions list and
loads after project trust is resolved, so it cannot handle `project_trust`. The CLI's built-in
extensions use it.

symbols.name: resourcePrecedenceRank
symbols.comment:
Compute a numeric precedence rank for a resource based on its metadata.
Lower rank = higher precedence. Used to sort resolved resources so that
name-collision resolution ("first wins") produces the correct outcome.

Precedence (highest to lowest):
  0  project + settings entry (source: "local", scope: "project")
  1  project + auto-discovered (source: "auto", scope: "project")
  2  user + settings entry (source: "local", scope: "user")
  3  user + auto-discovered (source: "auto", scope: "user")
  4  package resource (origin: "package")

symbols.comment:
Substitute argument placeholders in template content
Supports:
- $1, $2, ... for positional args
- $@ and $ARGUMENTS for all args
- ${N:-default} for positional arg N with default when missing/empty

- ${@:N} for args from Nth onwards (bash-style slicing)
- ${@:N:L} for L args starting from Nth

Note: Replacement happens on the template string only. Argument and default values
containing patterns like $1, $@, or $ARGUMENTS are NOT recursively substituted.

Optional default tool suppression mode when no explicit allowlist is provided.

symbols.name: CreateAgentSessionOptions.tools
symbols.comment:
Optional allowlist of tool names or patterns, where `*` matches any characters.

When omitted, pi uses the resolved `defaultTools` setting for the initial
selection when configured. Otherwise it enables the default built-in tools
(read, bash, edit, write). Extension/custom tools remain enabled unless
`noTools` changes that default. When provided, only matching tools are
enabled. MCP tools stay registered for codemode and tool search unless an
entry starts with `mcp__`; then only matching MCP tools are kept. An empty
list, like `noTools: "all"`, disables MCP tools too.

A list of only `+name` and `-name` entries is not an allowlist: it adds tools
to or removes them from the default selection, like the `defaultTools` setting.
These entries take exact names. Mixing them with plain entries throws.

symbols.name: CreateAgentSessionOptions.excludeTools
symbols.comment:

symbols.name: SessionManager
symbols.comment:
Manages conversation sessions as append-only trees stored in JSONL files.

Each session entry has an id and parentId forming a tree structure. The "leaf"
pointer tracks the current position. Appending creates a child of the current leaf.
Branching moves the leaf to an earlier entry, allowing new branches without
modifying history.

Use buildSessionContext() to get the resolved message list for the LLM, which
handles compaction summaries and follows the path from root to current leaf.

packages/coding-agent/src/core/virtual-m.comment:
Virtual models are catalog entries that route each request to a physical model.

The selection (`model_change`, `agent.state.model`, `ctx.model`) may name a virtual model.
Everything below the routing step only sees physical models: providers stream them and
assistant messages record them. A virtual model never reaches a provider.

separately and adds them to the provider's catalog with `withVirtualModels()`, so any provider,
including one with physical models, can list several virtual models.

packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/cod.comment:
The `codemode` tool: the model writes JavaScript that calls other tools. Scripts use `tools`,
`ALL_TOOLS`, `text()`, `image()`, `exit()`, `store()`/`load()`, `console.*`, and `return <value>`,
may start with a `// @options:` line, and reach the model catalog, classifiers, and image models
through `models.*`. Results start with a "Script completed" or "Script failed" header.

Scripts can call the agent loop's nested tools: active `direct` tools and every `codemode` or
`deferred` tool. Nested calls run through the agent loop's tool pipeline (`ctx.executeTool`), so
validation, `tool_call`/`tool_result` hooks, and permission checks apply exactly as for direct
calls. Only the script's output reaches the model; nested results do not.

Nested results are handed to the script as follows:
- A tool that declares `outputSchema` resolves to its `structuredContent`, also for error
  results that carry one.
- Any other tool resolves to its text content as one string.
- A failed, blocked, or invalid call rejects with an Error carrying the tool's error text.

A script that fails returns a normal error result that keeps its partial output, followed by
"Script error:" and the error. `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across
calls; successful scripts append their writes to the session as `codemode-store` custom entries,
so each branch sees the values written on its own path.

Worker entry for the codemode sandbox in bundled builds. The Node bundle and the Bun binary
build this file as a separate entrypoint because pi-codemode's own worker file is not on disk
there; `getCodemodeWorkerSpecifier()` in config.ts resolves it.

packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/mcp.comment:
MCP server configuration.

Servers are read from `mcp.json` in the agent directory and, for trusted projects, from
`<project>/.pi/mcp.json`. Both use the `mcpServers` shape shared by other MCP clients, so
existing configurations can be copied over. Project entries replace global entries with the
same name.

A project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and
`toolExposure` of the global server with the same name, for example to turn it off in one project:
`{ "mcpServers": { "internal-tools": { "enabled": false } } }`. The rest of the global entry is kept,
including credentials the project could not set itself.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."] },
    "docs": { "url": "https://example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}" } },
    "sentry": { "url": "https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp" }
  }
}
```

HTTP servers without an `Authorization` header use OAuth when they answer 401 (sign in with `/mcp`).
`"auth": { "provider": "<provider>" }` sends the token of a `/login` provider instead. Project files
cannot use it, so a repository cannot pick where the credential goes.

The top-level `autoEnableCodemode` (default true) activates the codemode tool when a server
with `codemode` exposure connects. A project value overrides the global one.

packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/mcp.comment:
Built-in MCP integration.

Connects the servers from `mcp.json` and the servers extensions register with
`pi.registerMcpServer()` when a session starts, and servers registered later right away. A server
in `mcp.json` takes precedence over a registered server of the same name. Connections run in the
background: the first prompt waits only for servers with `direct` tools, and codemode scripts,
`tool_search`, and the resource tools wait for the servers they need when they run. Tools are
registered as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. By default (`"exposure": "codemode"`) the tools are only
callable from codemode scripts, which keeps MCP tools out of the model's tool declarations and
the codemode description: scripts find the tools with `searchTools()` and the server instructions
with `describeNamespace()`. The codemode tool is activated for that unless `autoEnableCodemode` is
false. `"deferred"` declares the tools to the model once the `tool_search` tool loads them, and
activates `tool_search` instead of codemode.
`"exposure": "direct"` declares them to the model right away, and `"hidden"` makes them
unreachable. `toolExposure` overrides the exposure of single tools. Servers with resources are
reached through Codex's `list_mcp_resources`, `list_mcp_resource_templates`, and
`read_mcp_resource` tools (resources.ts).

Every call runs through pi's tool pipeline, so `tool_call`/`tool_result` hooks and permission
extensions apply to MCP tools the same way they do to built-in tools.

Problems found at startup (config errors, failed connections, servers that need a sign-in) are
reported once. `/mcp` opens a manager to sign in, reconnect, enable or disable servers, and change
their exposure; the last two are saved to the `mcp.json` that defines the server, or apply to the
current session for registered servers.

packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/mcp.comment:
OAuth sign-in for remote MCP servers: pi's credential store and its side of the sign-in.

Connections never start a browser flow on their own. They send the stored access token and, after
a 401, try the stored refresh token. When that is not possible they fail with
`McpOAuthAuthorizationRequiredError`, and the user signs in through `/mcp` or `pi mcp login`, which
run pi-mcp's sign-in (PKCE, pi's Client ID Metadata Document or dynamic client registration) against
a loopback callback or a pasted redirect URL.

Credentials live in `<agent-dir>/mcp-auth.json`, keyed by server name and URL.

MCP resources, through the tools Codex and opencode use: `list_mcp_resources`,
`list_mcp_resource_templates`, and `read_mcp_resource`. They take a `server` argument and cover
every connected server with resources, so models trained on those tools use them unchanged.

Listings are JSON, as in Codex: `{ server?, resources: [{ server, ...resource }], nextCursor? }`.
With a `server`, one page is listed and `cursor` continues it; without, every page of every server.
MCP App resources (`ui://` URIs and `profile=mcp-app` HTML) are left out, since they are user
interfaces for hosts that render them, and so are icons. Read resources become text and images for
the model; binary resources are saved to temp files. Scripts get the JSON payloads.

symbols.name: NAME_WEIGHT
symbols.comment:
A query term in the name counts this many times its IDF. The text part of a term is at most
`k1 + 1` (2.2) times its IDF and about 1 for a single mention, so a name match beats any number of
mentions in the description.

symbols.name: NAMESPACE_WEIGHT
symbols.comment:
A query term in the namespace name, description, or instructions counts this many times its IDF. They
are shared by every tool of the server, so they help find the server but not the tool in it.

symbols.name: Bm25Ranker
symbols.comment:
Okapi BM25 over the description, with the name and the namespace as separate fields:
- a tool that matches more of the query's terms, in any field, ranks above one that matches
  fewer, whatever their scores: for `screenshot window`, a tool whose description has both words
  beats `window`, whose name has one;
- a query term in the name scores more than any number of mentions in the description;
- a tool whose whole local name is in the query (`app` in `peekaboo app` for
  `mcp__peekaboo__app`) gets a bonus worth one more match of every query term, so among tools
  matching as many terms it mostly wins over tools that only mention the words;
- a query that is exactly a tool's name ranks that tool first, before coverage.

The description alone is length-normalized, so a long name or long namespace instructions do
not lower a tool's score. Ties keep document order.

symbols.name: Rgb
symbols.comment:
Fullscreen 3D easter eggs: the pi logo (header logo click) and Armin (/arminsayshi). Both are bitmaps built from
one block per pixel. The current screen dissolves into braille dust while the model spins in the center and its
blocks play a sliding puzzle. Leaving plays the same timeline backwards, so the screen reassembles.

The pi logo lifts off the header, flies to the center, and grows; the dust spreads out from the header logo.
Armin grows out of a speck at the center; the dust spreads out from the center.

The blocks are ray cast per braille dot. A braille cell holds 2x4 roughly square dots, so one pixel of a
half-block bitmap is exactly 2x2 dots, and the header logo (4x2 cells) is 8x8 dots when it lifts off.

symbols.name: ThemedText
symbols.comment:
Text whose content applies theme colors. Plain `Text` keeps the colors its string was built with, so
a theme change, or the system theme receiving the terminal's colors, would leave it stale. This
rebuilds the string from `build` after every invalidation, which the UI performs on theme changes.

`build` must return the same content each time, apart from colors. Snapshot changing data before
creating the component, or call `invalidate()` after changing state that `build` reads.

symbols.name: InteractiveMode.uncaughtCrash
symbols.comment:
Last-resort handler for uncaught exceptions. The TUI puts stdin into raw
mode and hides the cursor; without this handler, an uncaught throw from
anywhere (e.g. an extension's async `ChildProcess.on("exit")` callback)
tears down the process while leaving the terminal in raw mode with no
cursor, requiring `stty sane && reset` to recover.

Unlike emergencyTerminalExit, the terminal is still alive here, so we
call ui.stop() to restore cooked mode, the cursor, and disable bracketed
paste / Kitty / modifyOtherKeys sequences.

packages/coding-agent/src/modes/interact.comment:
The `system` theme: pi's colors derived from the terminal's own theme.

Every token belongs to a color family (its hue) and has contrast rules: it must reach a contrast level
on the background and on the panels it is drawn on. Hue and saturation come from the terminal's palette
color for the family's ANSI slot, or from the family's own hue when the terminal reports no palette.
Lightness comes from the rules alone. Colors are built in OKHSL, whose saturation is relative to the
sRGB gamut, and fade toward gray near black and white. A palette color never gains OKLCH chroma when it
moves to another lightness, so pastel palettes stay pastel.

A contrast level is a target-lightness curve: the OKLab lightness a token needs, given the lightness of
the surface below it. The curves were fitted to the reference theme design from the "Pi themes: system
and light/dark" review. On dark backgrounds they aim for nearly fixed lightness; on light backgrounds the
required difference grows as the background darkens.

Depending on what the terminal reports, the theme is generated in one of three tiers:
- background and palette: hues from the palette, lightness from the background;
- background only: the families' own hues, lightness from the background;
- nothing: ANSI palette indices and the default colors, which the terminal renders itself.

RPC mode: Headless operation with JSON stdin/stdout protocol.

Used for embedding the agent in other applications.
Receives commands as JSON on stdin, outputs events and responses as JSON on stdout.

- Commands: JSON objects with `type` field, optional `id` for correlation
- Responses: JSON objects with `type: "response"`, `command`, `success`, and optional `data`/`error`
- Events: AgentSessionEvent objects streamed as they occur
- Extension UI: Extension UI requests are emitted, client responds with extension_ui_response

waitForChildProcess
symbols.signature: export function waitForChildProcess(child: ChildProcess): Promise<number | null>
symbols.comment:
Wait for a child process to terminate without hanging on inherited stdio handles.

A short-lived child can `exit` while a detached descendant keeps its stdout/stderr
pipe open. We must not resolve and destroy the streams on a fixed deadline measured
from `exit`, or output still being written past that deadline is silently lost
(earendil-works/pi#5303). Instead, after `exit` we wait for the pipes to fall idle:
the grace timer is re-armed on every chunk, so an actively writing descendant keeps
us reading, while a quiet inherited handle (e.g. a Windows daemonized descendant
that never lets `close` fire) still releases us after the grace elapses.

packages/durable/src/codemode/codemode.t.comment:
Durable code mode: a tool that runs model-written JavaScript in a QuickJS sandbox, whose script survives a restart.

Problem: a script is in-memory VM state. A restart while

    const results = await Promise.all(paths.map((path) => tools.read({ path })));

waits for the last of 200 reads would lose the script and every read it made.

Solution: deterministic replay (`CodemodeSandboxBase.start()` in pi-codemode). The VM only runs when the host hands
it a result; given the same start data, clock, seed, and results in the same order, it makes the same calls with
the same arguments. The tool is replay-safe: after a restart, `execute()` runs again, starts the script again from
the stored start data, and hands it the results it got before, in the order it got them, from a journal written
before each delivery. Nested tool calls reattach to their tasks by key (`c<VM call id>`), so they never run twice
unless their own replay policy reruns them; their results come from `NestedCallDoc`. Then the script continues live.

Documents, scoped to the code mode call's task and gone when it settles:
- `pi.codemode.run`: the start data, written once before the VM starts, and the outcome, written once when the call
  decides it (with the store writes, in one transaction), so a rerun after that returns it without a VM.
- `pi.codemode.journal`: one entry per delivered result, in delivery order: the VM call ID, the clock value, the
  calls the VM had issued after processing it (once acknowledged), and a global's outcome, which nothing else stores.

Each result's acknowledged call count is recorded with the next journal commit, or at once when the VM has processed
everything delivered: a script waiting on a long call is where a restart usually finds it. A sequential script
therefore costs one journal commit and one count commit per result, on top of its nested calls' own; that is the
price of checking the most common crash point.

A call is launched only once the count of calls issued in the drain that made it is committed. So every key an earlier
attempt admitted is at most its last recorded count; a replay checks every recorded count, so when it releases its
calls it has made every call an earlier attempt could have admitted, and later calls are new.

A rerun refuses to replay (no new nested calls; nested calls admitted earlier may still resume on their own and are
aborted by the call's cleanup) when this module's version or the VM's fingerprint changed, when the deadline passed,
or when the script diverges: it makes another call, or calls in another order, than the journal says. Each ends the
call with an error result.

symbols.name: NodeFileWatcher
symbols.comment:
Watches by snapshots: native events only trigger a debounced rescan, and changes are the difference between
snapshots plus the event paths. A replaced file, a renamed or recreated ancestor, or a directory created with its
contents therefore never depends on which events an operating system sends. New directories get their watchers
before they are scanned again, so nothing written into them before the watcher existed is missed.

The message of a thrown value, without throwing itself: `String()` throws for values such as `Object.create(null)`,
and code that formats an error must not fail for the value it formats.

symbols.name: ReadAfterWrite
symbols.comment:
A transaction read a table after its first table write, or admitted a submission (`submit(tx, draft)`) after it. Read
every required row, and admit, before writing.

symbols.name: StorageRequestError
symbols.comment:
A Storage read rejected an invalid request, such as an unknown conversation or a cursor from another scan, with no
durable effect. Unlike any other error a Storage throws, it fails only that read, not the Session; from `commit()` it is
fatal like any other.

symbols.name: SessionFailed
symbols.comment:
The Session failed, so nothing runs or commits any more. It fails when a Storage method throws, a commit cannot be
adopted, or the Harness's own bookkeeping throws (a scheduler commit, an internal commit listener, a registry whose
`snapshot()` throws). `cause` is that first error. Reopen the Session; reopening recovers from what was committed.

symbols.name: ReadOnlySession
symbols.comment:
The Harness was opened read-only (`HarnessOptions.readOnly`): a commit with writes, or a call that would run tasks, was
refused. Nothing was written, and the Harness stays usable for reads.

symbols.comment:
`addTools` of a tool round, applied to `tools` and `modelTools`, so the next request offers the tools: an array gets
each name it lacks appended, and `{ remove }` loses the names. An unset `tools` already enables every tool, so nothing
is written for it. An unset or object `modelTools` also gets each name appended to its `add`, which loads deferred

symbols.name: CompactionTask
symbols.comment:
Built-in compaction task (spec §8.7): select an old prefix of the model context, summarize it, and place a summary
entry whose `head` is the first kept entry. A compaction the generation owns blocks it and appends directly; a
conversation-owned one places its summary through a write submission.

symbols.name: createCompaction
symbols.comment:
Create a compaction task with its status in this commit. `owner` is the generation that waits for it (a blocking
compaction); without one it is conversation-owned, and `background` unless it is manual.

symbols.name: compactionPolicy
symbols.comment:
The compaction policy for `model` in a conversation, field by field: the conversation's `modelOverrides` entry, the
harness's, the conversation's own fields, then the harness-wide policy. A model-specific value beats a general one,
and the conversation beats the harness at the same level. The exception: the conversation's own `enabled: false` also
beats the harness's model override, since turning compaction off for a conversation does not depend on the model.

symbols.comment:
Index in `view.entries` of the first entry a summary keeps, or `undefined` when there is nothing to compact
(spec §8.7). Walks back from the tail until `keepRecentTokens` are kept, then cuts at the first candidate at or after
that entry: an entry whose contribution starts with a user or assistant message, never a tool result, and never a
user entry that a result of the preceding assistant's calls still follows.

symbols.name: serializeConversation
symbols.signature: export function serializeConversation(messages: readonly Message[]): string
symbols.comment:
Messages as plain text, so the summarizer reads a transcript instead of continuing it. System messages are omitted.
Thinking is omitted too: providers return summaries of the real reasoning, and replayed thinking is often not part of
the live context (a block that does not match its request is dropped), so including it can make the request larger
than the context it summarizes. Visible text, tool calls, and tool results record what happened.

symbols.name: captureContextBounds
symbols.comment:
Capture the bounds of the current context, or of the context cut off at the visible entry `at`. The newest entry
and head marker are known from the Session's commits, so the current bounds usually cost no Storage read. Run this
on the Session line; entries at or below the tail are immutable, so `deriveContext()` can then scan them off the
line.

symbols.comment:
One context read: the visible entries it scanned, from the head marker's head, or transcript start, through
`bounds.tail`, oldest first, and the view derived from them. Entries at or below the tail never change, so a later
read with the same head marker extends both.

symbols.comment:
`view.messages` from the contributed messages before the last assistant message. Tool results are ordered within
the messages up to the next assistant message, so later entries cannot change these.

symbols.name: open
symbols.comment: Contributed messages from the last assistant message on, before tool result ordering.

symbols.name: baseline
symbols.comment: The baseline's system message; see `findBaseline()`.

symbols.name: current
symbols.comment:
Whether the range reached the conversation's newest entry when it was read, so the entries of later commits extend
it (`advanceRange()`); a range cut off at an earlier entry is not.

symbols.name: Baseline
symbols.comment: A baseline's system message, `null` when the range cannot have one, or `undefined` while a later entry may be one.

export async function readContextFrom(

	conversationId: ConversationId,

	at: EntryId | undefined,
	previous: ContextRange | undefined,

symbols.comment:
`readContext()` that reuses `previous`, an earlier range of the same conversation: with the same head marker, only
entries after its tail are scanned. Returns the view and the range to pass to the next read. A range outlives the
read, so its entries are frozen like `MemoryStorage` records, and the returned view has its own arrays. A caller that
keeps the range for `advanceRange()` checks `current` again, synchronously where it installs it: a commit can be
published between this function's return and the caller's continuation.

symbols.name: deriveContext
symbols.comment:
Derive the active transcript and model context of one conversation within captured bounds.

H = newest visible head marker; the range runs from `H.head` (or transcript start) through the tail. Per target,
the newest edit in the range wins. Context entries are H followed by the range's non-head entries.

symbols.name: rangeEntry
symbols.signature: export function rangeEntry(range: ContextRange, id: EntryId): EntryRecord | undefined
symbols.comment: Entry `id` of `range`, by binary search: a range holds its entries in ID order, every one visible from its conversation.

symbols.name: advanceRange
symbols.signature: export function advanceRange(range: ContextRange, appended: readonly EntryRecord[]): ContextRange | undefined
symbols.comment:
`range` with the entries one commit appended to its conversation, in ID order, without reading Storage: the
conversation's own new entries are its newest, and a new head marker's head never lies before the range's start.
A range that is not `current` stays as it is; the next read extends it from Storage. `undefined` drops the range.

symbols.name: deriveRange
symbols.signature: function deriveRange(bounds: ContextBounds, entries: readonly EntryRecord[], current: boolean): ContextRange
symbols.comment: Derive the context view from the entries scanned within `bounds`.

symbols.name: extendRange
symbols.comment:
`previous` extended by the entries `added` after its tail under the same head marker: only their contributions and
the open messages are derived. An added edit can change an earlier entry, so it derives the whole range again.

symbols.name: findBaseline
symbols.signature: function findBaseline(head: ContextBounds["head"], entries: readonly EntryRecord[]): Baseline
symbols.comment:
The baseline among `entries`, oldest first: the system message of the first `pi.system` entry after the head
marker, or of the transcript without one, when generation wrote it with every section and tool in effect. After a
head marker it always does, and omits the retained `pi.system` entries. Without one it does when it saw no system
message before, which holds unless an earlier entry carries one, even if an edit omits it later. An edit that targets
the baseline contributes other messages, or none, so none leads; a later entry does not take its place.

symbols.name: carriesSystemMessage
symbols.comment: Whether an entry's own messages, or the replacement messages of its edits, include a system message.

symbols.name: leadWithSystem
symbols.signature: function leadWithSystem(messages: Message[], baseline: Baseline): Message[]
symbols.comment:
Move the first system message to the front when only user messages precede it, or when it is the baseline's. A run's
input is committed before generation renders the system prompt, so a transcript starts with the input followed by
the baseline, and the range after a compaction with the kept history, assistant messages included. Providers treat
only a leading system message as the initial prompt and tool set; without it, a later tool change rewrites the
request's tool list and invalidates the whole prompt cache. Only the first system message moves, so replaying
system messages in order gives the same sections and tools. Any other system message, before an assistant message,
stays where it was committed: moving it would change what it means to the model.

symbols.name: contribute
symbols.signature: function contribute(entry: EntryRecord, edit: ContextEdit | undefined): readonly Message[]
symbols.comment: One active entry's model messages after its edit and excluded stop reasons, before tool result ordering.

symbols.name: deeplyFrozen
symbols.comment: Objects `freezeJson()` froze with everything in them. `Object.isFrozen()` holds for shallow freezes too.

symbols.name: freezeJson
symbols.comment: Freeze a JSON value and everything in it.

symbols.name: settle
symbols.comment:
Move the ordered messages before the last assistant message of `open` to `settled`. `orderToolResults()` of a
sequence equals the concatenation over its parts when each later part starts with an assistant message.

symbols.name: assignJson
symbols.comment:
Assign `value` at `target[key]` leaf by leaf. Chord records a container assignment as one full set and only emits an
append when a string leaf is reassigned with a longer string, so writing the partial whole would store and publish the
complete message on every flush. That append costs a compare of the whole string, though; where `plan` says what a
string member grew by, and the committed string plus that text has the new string's length, the text is appended

symbols.name: settleSchedulerOutcome
symbols.comment:
Harness cleanup for a terminal outcome the scheduler writes itself (`faulted` or `orphaned`). A run task ends its
run; a tool task's slot is marked done without an entry, and context derivation synthesizes the missing result; a
compaction task's status is removed and its failure recorded.
Ignores other kinds so it never creates `pi.live` elsewhere. The scheduler calls this without knowing task kinds;
the Harness passes it in (spec §5.4).
REMINDER: a committed generation partial becomes an aborted assistant entry here, exactly as in the generation abort
handler, so the transcript keeps what the model produced and `pi.usage` counts its spend. The scheduler's commit has
no task scope, so that entry has no `byTaskId`. Faults come from task bugs
or malformed provider data (a non-JSON value in a response), or a commit the Storage rejected without effect; an
uncertain storage failure poisons the Session instead and writes no outcome.

symbols.name: PartialChanges
symbols.comment:
Collects, from a response's events, what changed in its partial message since the last commit, so the commit appends
new text instead of reassigning growing strings. Reassigning makes Chord compare the old and new string, which costs
O(length) per commit.

- Text and thinking: the `text_delta` and `thinking_delta` events. The commit appends them where the committed string
  plus the deltas has the new string's length, and compares otherwise. A block's `*_end` event drops them, because
  providers may replace the text when a block ends.
- Tool-call arguments: a `StreamingJsonParser` per call, fed with the raw argument text of each `toolcall_delta`,
  reports what each piece changed. The commit applies those changes to the committed arguments in order and leaves
  the arguments out of the message assignment, so the committed arguments are exactly the parsed text so far.
  `toolcall_end` ends the tracking; the call's last commit assigns its final arguments.

Take what changed since the last call, for a commit of `message`, a copy of the partial. Clears the arguments of
tracked tool calls in `message`: the commit writes them from the changes. Call `restore()` if the commit fails.

commit(

- A head marker with no later `pi.system` entry in context: one complete baseline that omits every retained earlier

symbols.name: readOnly
symbols.comment:
`HarnessOptions.readOnly`: open loads live tasks as committed, `running` ones included, and the scheduler never
commits, runs anything, or asks for a wakeup.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler
symbols.comment:
Durable task scheduler of one Harness.

`#live` mirrors every committed non-terminal task record: pending, running, waiting, sleeping, and completing. The
synchronous commit listener updates it on the Session line, so code running on the line reads exactly the committed
state from it.

Tasks and conversations form one ownership tree (spec §5.5): a task's parent is its owner task, or its conversation;
a conversation's parent is its owner task, if any. Walks up that tree decide what reaches one task: a cancelling
owner, a scope. `#below` lists the tree downward around live work, so what lies below one node is a walk down from
it: a task's live ordinary owned work, which holds its outcome as `completing` and delays its abort handler, a
scope's tasks, a cascade's reach. No pass visits every live task; the sets below hold each pass's candidates.

The ownership indexes are bounded by live work: an owner edge and an ended task's ownership fields are kept only while
something is listed below them in `#below`, so only the chains above live tasks are known, whole. Work that appears
later below a dropped node finds it unknown and loads its chain from storage again.

Invariant: every task transition is decided and written by one callback serialized on the Session line. That covers
reservation, marks, runtime commits, finalization, and the step before each phase, which applies the precedence rules
and writes a fault or handover. Handlers and joins run off the line. An invocation ends inside the step that decides
its end, so a runtime commit it queued either lands before that decision or is rejected.

Decisions stay serialized; their storage overlaps (group commit). The Session stores the commits of several jobs in
one call while the line runs on, and this memory changes only as each commit is published. So every decision reads
it in a decision region (`#region()`): synchronous, recording the keys it reads (a task's record, the live work below
a node, the cancellation intent set), staging nothing; when one of them has an unpublished writer, the region waits
for its publication and runs again, and only a region that read nothing unpublished is applied. Every commit writes
the memberships its task changes alter (`membershipKeys()`), so a walk that a pending commit would change waits.

Context range last read through a task runtime, per conversation: a later read, by any of its tasks, scans only
newer entries. `idleSince` is the Harness time it was first seen idle. Derived and never persisted; dropped at the
first idle check after `settings.contextRetentionMs` of idleness, and at close.

scans `#contexts`. Kept sorted also when the Harness clock goes back (see `#markIdle`).

A chain load resolved what `#idle()` treats as unknown for a live task whose chain is not loaded, which can make a
scope idle without a task change below it; the next idle check then covers every scope.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#fullIdleChecks

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#settled
symbols.comment: Ownership fields of the known terminal tasks, which walks pass through.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#dropQueue
symbols.comment:
Ended tasks and conversations found unneeded, dropped by `#sweep()` at the end of the commit's publication unless
needed again by then: a chain load installs nodes before the work below them is listed.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#below
symbols.comment:
The tree downward around live work: each node's child nodes that are live tasks or have nodes listed below them.
A conversation's parent is its owner task; ownerless ones with work are in `#roots`.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#unloaded
symbols.comment: Known tasks whose chain may not be loaded; every other known task's chain is, and stays, loaded.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#intent
symbols.comment: Live tasks with cancellation intent, the sources of abort cascades (spec §5.4).

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#runnable
symbols.comment: Live tasks that are not `completing`, the candidates of a reservation pass; ones found waiting leave it.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#finalizeChecks
symbols.comment: `completing` tasks the next finalize pass checks: those that started holding, and holders of ended work.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#waiters
symbols.comment: Live waiting tasks by each task in their `on`.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#failFastChecks
symbols.comment:
`failFast` waiters the next reconcile checks for a failed task in `on`: at open, when they start waiting, and when
one of their tasks fails.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#abandoned
symbols.comment:
Live tasks with `abandonOnRestart` found at open, from an earlier Harness. The first reservation pass abort-marks
them with reason `restart`, so nothing of them or below them runs a phase again.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#sleeping
symbols.comment: Sleeping live tasks, due or not: the candidates of `#wakeDue()`.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#timer
symbols.signature: #timer: { readonly at: number; readonly disarm: () => void } | undefined;

symbols.output: { readonly at: number; readonly disarm: () => void } | undefined

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#lastWake
symbols.comment: Last value given to `onWake`, so an unchanged one is not repeated.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#snapshotReported
symbols.comment: A registry snapshot that threw for the task graph was reported; it is read per record, so only once.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#reconcilingWork
symbols.comment: Reconcile passes underway with work (they may overlap): their commits finalize held outcomes and mark cascades.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#pins
symbols.comment:
Nodes chain loads installed for jobs whose commits are not published yet, with how many such jobs: the sweep keeps
them, as work a pending commit creates below them needs them.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#reading
symbols.comment: Keys the decision region underway reads (`#region()`); set only while one runs.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.open
TaskScheduler.resume
symbols.comment:
Enable scheduling, and make sleeping tasks that are due runnable: a host wakeup, such as an alarm, calls this.
Idempotent; the kick does nothing once closing.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.blockedReason
symbols.comment:
Why a live task cannot run here, if it cannot: its definition is missing, too old, or failed to migrate. A running
task, an abort-marked one, and one holding its outcome are never blocked.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.subscribeBlocked
symbols.comment: Call `listener` when blocked reasons may have changed without a commit: a registry change or a failed migration.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.wake
symbols.comment:
When the Session next needs a process: `active` while some task can run now or is running, `at` for the earliest
sleep not yet due. Synchronous, from memory; a task whose chain is not loaded yet counts as it would alone.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#runsNow
symbols.comment: Whether a live task can run now: the scan `wake()` needs only while no invocation runs.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.join
symbols.comment:
Signal every invocation and wait for them, then write the tasks they ran back as `pending` (`writeAtClose`), as a
close is not a crash. Close calls this after every close listener has run, so waits, watches, and streams a task
holds end with the Session's reason, not as cancelled by its signal.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.abort
symbols.signature: async abort(id: TaskId, context: Context, keepRestart = false): Promise<"marked" | "terminal">
symbols.comment:
Commit the abort mark, or settle a task that no registered definition can take as `orphaned` when nothing it owns
is live, then join the run invocation seen on the line; the commit listener signalled it. The abort invocation
starts once the task's ordinary owned work is gone. A `completing` task is only marked. A request replaces a
`restart` mark, so a task abandoned after a restart that waits for its definition is orphaned; with `keepRestart`,
as for an owner's own cleanup, such a task keeps its mark and waits on.

symbols.comment:
Resolve when ordinary traversal from the conversation, or from every ownerless conversation, reaches no live
non-background task.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.abortConversation
symbols.signature: async abortConversation(conversationId: ConversationId, background: boolean, context: Context): Promise<void>
symbols.comment:
`Conversation.abort()`: in one commit, withdraw the queued inputs and mark every live non-background task that
ordinary traversal from the conversation reaches; resolves once the scope is idle. With `background`, traversal
crosses background boundaries, and the wait also covers every task it reached.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.membershipKeys
symbols.signature: membershipKeys(tx: Transaction): readonly string[] | Promise<readonly string[]>
symbols.comment:
The ownership memberships a commit's task and conversation changes write (group commit §4.2), at its admission on
the line: for each task created or made terminal, every node from its parent up to and including the nearest live
task, or the root conversation, and then the roots too, conservatively, as a pending end may unlist the root a
creation finds listed; for each conversation created under a task, that task; and the intent set when
a change sets, upgrades, or clears a mark or a held or ended outcome other than `completed`. Loads the chains it
walks; the nodes it installs stay until the commit is published.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#membershipKeys
symbols.signature:
async #membershipKeys(

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#chainKeys
symbols.signature:
async #chainKeys(
		start: Node,
		overlay: Overlay,
		keys: Set<string>,
		reached: Map<string, ConversationId | undefined>,
	): Promise<ConversationId | undefined>
symbols.comment:
Add the memberships from `start` up to and including the nearest live task, or the root conversation, which it
returns. `reached` keeps, per node walked, where its walk ended, so a chain several tasks of a commit share is
walked once. Whether an ancestor is live can change under a pending commit, so it is read after a touch of the
ancestor's record: a pending end must not stop the chain early. Ownership fields are immutable, so not keyed.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#addScopesAbove
symbols.comment:
Add the conversations above `record` to `scopes`: those whose idleness a change of it can change. False when a node
on the way up is not known. A conversation already in `scopes` has everything above it there too.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#advanceContexts
symbols.comment:
Extend each kept context range with the entries a stored commit appended to its conversation, so a later read
needs no Storage scan. Entries are published in ID order.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#contextRetentionMs
symbols.comment:
`settings.contextRetentionMs`, or 0 when the host's settings throw. Kept contexts are only a cache, so dropping them
is safe, while a throw here would escape commit listeners, reconciliation, and the expiry timer.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#settleIdle
symbols.comment:
After task changes below the conversations in `scopes` (every conversation when undefined): resolve their idle
waiters and the Harness-wide ones, drop the kept contexts whose idle period passed the retention, then start or end
the idle periods of the kept contexts in `scopes`. A task change can change the idleness only of the conversations
above it, so no check visits every conversation.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#resolveIdleWaiters
symbols.comment: Resolve the idle waiters of the conversations in `scopes` (all when undefined) and the Harness-wide ones.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#expireContexts
symbols.comment:
Drop the kept contexts idle for at least `retention`, oldest first, with the retention setting of now; with no
retention, every idle one, also those whose idle period a clock that went back makes start after now.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#markIdle
symbols.comment:
Start the idle period of a kept context in the expiry order. An idle period older than the newest one kept, which
a clock that went back starts, sorts the order again, and the newest is taken from what is kept then.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#dropContext
symbols.comment: Forget a kept context, idle or not, and its place in the expiry order.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#scheduleExpiry
symbols.comment:
Drop the expired contexts when the earliest idle context expires, on a background timer, which never keeps the
process alive. Where the host declines it, as the default does in Cloudflare Workers, none is kept: a pending timer
could keep a Durable Object from being evicted, and eviction frees the contexts. There, task changes alone check
expiry.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#reconcile
symbols.comment:
One commit that applies what committed records imply: abort marks below live owners with cancellation intent
(spec §5.4), `failFast` marks (spec §5.5), withdrawn queued inputs below cancelled owners, and the final terminal
record of every `completing` task whose ordinary owned work is gone. The durable records are the intent, so this
also repairs whatever a crash left unapplied. Resolves idle waiters that the loaded edges decide.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#marks
symbols.signature: async #marks(): Promise<Map<TaskId, { readonly record: AnyTaskRecord; readonly reason: "restart" | undefined }>>
symbols.comment:
The abort marks committed records imply (spec §5.4, §5.5): every live foreground task below a live owner with
cancellation intent, which is its nearest one (a walk down from each owner with intent does not enter another,
whose own walk covers what is below it), and every other live task in the `on` of a `failFast` waiter one of whose
tasks failed. A cascade from an abandoned owner passes its `restart` reason on; any other intent marks, or upgrades
a `restart` mark, as a request. Collected first, so a request wins over a `restart` mark of the same pass. Derived
again on every pass, as loading edges can reveal a cancelled owner. Takes the `failFast` checks once its decision
stands.
symbols.output: Promise<Map<TaskId, { readonly record: AnyTaskRecord; readonly reason: "restart" | undefined }>>

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#planMarks
symbols.comment: `#marks()`' decision region; the `failFast` members it needs from Storage first, when `ended` lacks them.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.marks
symbols.signature: readonly marks: Map<TaskId, { readonly record: AnyTaskRecord; readonly reason: "restart" | undefined }>;
symbols.output: Map<TaskId, { readonly record: AnyTaskRecord; readonly reason: "restart" | undefined }>

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#reconcileWork
symbols.comment: Whether a reconcile pass would have work: a cascade to derive, held outcomes to check, or `failFast` waits.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#finalize
symbols.comment:
Write the terminal record of every `completing` task without live ordinary owned work. Finalizing one can free its
owner, so this repeats over the commit's candidates until nothing changes. A held scheduler outcome gets its
Harness cleanup here. In rounds, one decision region each: the holders the tasks of one round free are checked once,
in the next, so a holder of many tasks that end together is walked once, not once per task. The first round takes
the `completing` tasks to check once its decision stands.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#planRound
symbols.comment:
One finalize round's decision: which of `ids` are `completing` without live ordinary owned work below them, in the
commit's candidates with the round's own finalizations applied in order, and the holders above them to check next.
Tasks finalized have no live work below them, so walks down skip them. It applies the round's terminal records to
`overlay` while it decides and takes them back before it returns, so a run again starts from the same candidates.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.finalized
symbols.signature: readonly finalized: readonly { readonly record: AnyTaskRecord; readonly terminal: AnyTaskRecord }[];
symbols.output: readonly { readonly record: AnyTaskRecord; readonly terminal: AnyTaskRecord }[]

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#loadScopes
symbols.comment:
Load the owner chains of the tasks in `#unloaded` and, with `queued`, of every conversation with queued inputs,
on the Session line; returns the latter. Reads through the line's Storage, so it may run inside a commit callback.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#loadChain
symbols.comment:
Load the owner edges and task nodes from `start` up to its ownerless root. A known task outside `#unloaded` ends the
walk, as its chain is loaded; the `#unloaded` tasks passed have a loaded chain afterwards. Loading a node can reveal
a cancelled owner, so it makes the next reconcile derive cascade marks. The nodes it installs stay until the job's
commit is published (`#pin()`).

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#liveUnloaded
symbols.comment: Whether a live task's chain is not loaded yet: one `#idle()` counts as inside every scope it may be in.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#settle
symbols.comment: Know a terminal task a chain load read, so walks pass through it; its own chain is not loaded yet.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#dropIfUnneeded
symbols.comment: Queue an ended task or a conversation for the sweep when nothing is listed below it.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#scheduleSweep
symbols.comment:
Sweep in a job of its own on the Session line, after the operation underway: a rejected commit, one with nothing to
write, and a read publish nothing, so the sweep at the end of `#observe` would not run for what they loaded.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#sweep
symbols.comment:
Drop the queued nodes that are still unneeded: not live, nothing listed below. Runs once a publication is fully
tracked, and as a job of its own on the line, never inside an operation: work a commit creates below a chain its
own callback loaded keeps that chain. A flat loop: unlisting already queued every node on the way up that lost its
last listed node.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#region
symbols.comment:
Run `decide`, a decision region (group commit §6): synchronous, reading scheduler memory and recording the keys it
reads, staging nothing and changing no scheduler state. When a key it read has an unpublished writer, its result,
or its error, is dropped: once that writer is published, `refresh` reloads what the region needs and it runs
again. A waiting job holds the line, so unpublished writes only shrink, and the runs converge. What a region read
that had no unpublished writer gets none for the rest of the job, so its result stands while the job applies it.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#reloadScopes
symbols.comment: Load the chains a region walks, again after it waited: what was published meanwhile may list new work.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#record
symbols.comment: In a decision region, note that it reads `key`; anywhere else, nothing.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#liveRecord
symbols.comment: A live task's committed record, read by a decision region.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#pin
symbols.comment:
Keep `node`, which a chain load of the job on the line installed, until that job's commit is published or fails:
work it creates below the node needs it, and the sweep would drop it as unneeded before then.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#track
symbols.comment:
Bring the scheduler's sets in line with a task's committed record. A task that ended may free the nearest live task
above it: one holding its outcome finalizes, an abort-marked one runs its abort handler; its waiters may run.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#release
symbols.comment: The nearest live task above ended ordinary work may be free now: one holding its outcome, or an aborting one.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#relist
symbols.comment:
List `start` under its parent node in `#below` while it is a live task or has nodes listed below it, and unlist it
otherwise; then its parent, as far up as that changes. So `#below` holds exactly the tree around live work; a
parent that loses its last listed node is queued for the sweep. A loop, as ownership chains can be deeper than the
call stack.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#nearestLiveAbove
symbols.comment:
The nearest live task above ended ordinary work `node`, in the overlay's view: the one that work held, if any. Work
at or below a background task holds nothing above it.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#known
symbols.comment: Whether the chain above `node` is loaded, without walking: known tasks outside `#unloaded` have a loaded chain.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#edge
symbols.signature: #edge(id: ConversationId, overlay?: Overlay): TaskId | null | undefined
symbols.comment: Owner task of a conversation, `null` when ownerless, `undefined` while not loaded.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#above
symbols.comment: Walk up from `start`: owner tasks and conversations, ending at an ownerless root or an edge not loaded yet.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#walkDown
symbols.comment:
The tasks below `start` that a walk down reaches: those `#below` lists and, under an overlay, the commit's new tasks,
with its candidates in place of committed records. Background tasks are reached but not entered, unless
`crossBackground`, and neither are the tasks `enter` rejects. A loop, as chains can be deeper than the call stack.
symbols.output: Generator<{ readonly id: TaskId; readonly node: TaskNode; readonly live: AnyTaskRecord | undefined }>

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#links
symbols.comment:
The links walks down need for the commit's new tasks: each one under its parent node, then each node above it that
`#below` does not list yet, until one it lists, a live task (always listed), or the chain's end.

#ownedLive(

symbols.signature: #inScope(start: Up, scope: Scope, crossBackground = false): boolean | undefined
symbols.comment:
Whether ordinary traversal from `scope` reaches `start`: walking up reaches the scope's conversation, or an
ownerless one for `roots`, without crossing a background owner, unless `crossBackground`. `undefined` while an
edge is not loaded.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#belowCancelled
symbols.comment:
Whether a live owner's cancellation intent reaches `start`: walking up finds an owner with intent before a
background owner without it. Terminal owners never cascade (spec §5.4).

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#cancellingOwner
symbols.comment: The nearest live owner above `start` whose cancellation intent reaches it, if any; see `#belowCancelled`.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#countActive
symbols.comment:
Count a task in or out of `pi.durable.tasks.active`. Commit observers count at a commit's publication, which must not
throw, so a throwing adapter is reported.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#failSession
symbols.comment: Fail the Session, which reports it, for a throw in one of the scheduler's own commits; ignored once closing.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#seal
symbols.comment: Close listener: runs synchronously once admission is sealed, before `join()`, or when the Session fails.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#scheduleWake
symbols.comment:
Recompute the wake in a microtask the line never waits for, with no order relative to host commit listeners (one
already queued serves later changes too): arm the built-in timer, or tell `onWake` of a change.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#armTimer
symbols.comment:
Keep the timer for the earliest sleep. It keeps the process alive, unlike the context expiry timer: a process with a
sleeping task has work left, such as a retry backoff. Rechecks the clock when it fires, so a wake before `until`
only arms it again.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#wakeDue
symbols.comment: Make every sleeping task whose time has come a reservation candidate.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#aboutTask
symbols.comment:
The report info of a task's failure, with the extension that installed its definition: the code that failed is
that extension's. Built-in tasks have none.

What a report about `task`'s own code says of it: the task, and the extension that installed its definition.
symbols.output: { readonly task: ReportTask; readonly extension?: string }

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.extension
symbols.comment: The installer of the definition whose code ran (an invocation's); absent: the current one's.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#restartLimit
symbols.comment: `settings.restartLimit`, or the default when the host's settings throw.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#notDue
symbols.comment: A sleep whose `until` the clock has not reached; an abort mark ends a sleep.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.state
symbols.signature: readonly state: { readonly status: "sleeping"; readonly until: number }

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#reserve
symbols.comment:
Reserve every eligible task in one commit; orphan abort-marked tasks no definition can take, unless abandoned after
a restart. The first pass after open only abort-marks the abandoned tasks, so later passes see the marks.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#planReservation
symbols.comment:
A reservation pass's decision region: the candidates it drops (gone, holding, waiting, asleep, or with an
invocation), whether one waits for a cascade, and the runnable records to resolve. Iterating the candidates is not
keyed: a pass that misses a task a pending commit makes runnable only delays it, as does skipping one with an
invocation without reading its record, or a waiter's check whether what it waits on is still live.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#waitingOn
symbols.comment:
Live tasks a task waits for before its next invocation: its live ordinary owned work when abort-marked, since
abort runs bottom-up, otherwise the live part of the `on` of a wait.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#resolve
symbols.comment: Resolve the record's definition by kind, migrating an older stored version.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.indexSizes
symbols.comment: Sizes of the ownership indexes, for tests that bound the scheduler's memory.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#step
symbols.signature:
async #step(
		invocation: Invocation,
		plan: (current: ErasedRunningTask) => StepPlan,
		progress?: (tx: Transaction, current: ErasedRunningTask) => boolean,
	): Promise<ErasedRunningTask | undefined>
symbols.comment:
One decision on the Session line, before a phase: a decision region (`#region()`) that reads the task's record. A
task that is no longer running (rule 1: terminal, `completing`, `waiting`, or `sleeping`) or a closing Harness (rule
2) ends the invocation without a write; otherwise `plan` decides, and a decision that stands is applied: the
invocation continues, with `progress` for rule 5, or ends, with a fault written. Ending happens inside the callback,
before a fault's Harness cleanup. A rejected step, such as admission after close, also ends the invocation. Its
outcome goes to the invocation only, so it is a scheduler commit (`commitInternal()`).

its Harness cleanup waits for the final commit (spec §5.5, rule 4); otherwise it is terminal with its cleanup.

async #commitState(
		tx: Transaction,
		invocation: Invocation,
		current: ErasedRunningTask,
		next: NextTaskState<Checkpoint, JsonValue>,
	): Promise<void>
symbols.comment:
Replace a running task's state with what it committed. A terminal state holds as `completing` while ordinary owned
work is live, judged on the commit's candidates, so work the same commit creates below the task counts. A wait is
validated first.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#validateWait
symbols.signature:
async #validateWait(
		tx: Transaction,
		invocation: Invocation,
		current: ErasedRunningTask,
		on: readonly TaskId[],
		policy: string,
	): Promise<void>
symbols.comment:
A wait names existing tasks, and `failFast` only tasks the waiter owns. It may not close a cycle in the wait-for
graph, whose edges run from each task to what it waits on and to its live ordinary owned work (spec §5.5); waiting
on itself or on an owner holding it are the shortest such cycles. An abort handler cannot wait.

Invariant: the wait-for graph is acyclic. Only a wait adds an edge between existing tasks, as a new task has only
incoming edges, so checking each wait maintains it.

#checkWait(
		current: ErasedRunningTask,
		on: readonly TaskId[],
		policy: string,
		overlay: Overlay,
		ended: ReadonlyMap<TaskId, AnyTaskRecord | null>,
	): { readonly missing: readonly TaskId[] } | { readonly error: Error } | undefined
symbols.comment:
`#validateWait()`'s decision region: why the wait is refused, `undefined` when it may be stored, or the tasks in
`on` it needs from Storage first, when `ended` lacks them.

symbols.name: TaskScheduler.#waitCycle
symbols.signature: #waitCycle(task: TaskId, on: readonly TaskId[], overlay: Overlay): TaskId[] | undefined
symbols.comment:
The path from a member of `on` back to `task` in the wait-for graph, if the wait would close a cycle (spec §5.1).
An edge X -> Y means X cannot settle before Y: Y is in the `on` of waiting X that is not abort-marked, or Y is live
ordinary owned work of X, which holds X as `completing`. Each task is visited once and each subtree walked once,
so a check is bounded by the live work it reaches. Part of a decision region: it records every record it reads.
Owned work is found by walks down, which need the chains of every live task loaded.

symbols.name: admitSubmission
symbols.signature:
export async function admitSubmission(
	tx: Tx,
	conversationId: ConversationId,
	draft: SubmissionDraft,
	now: number,
	queueModes: QueueModes,
	span?: TelemetrySpan,
): Promise<Admission>
symbols.comment:
Admit a submission inside a commit (spec §6); both `Conversation.submit()` forms and conversation-owned compactions
share it. A known request ID returns its existing submission without writing. A display-only write (only `kind` and
`data`) is appended and settled `done` at once, busy or not, as it changes nothing the model sees; only behind a
queued reset it queues, so it lands after the reset instead of before it in the context the reset ends. A busy
conversation queues anything else in `pi.inbox`, or rejects `whenBusy: "reject"` input and any continue with
`ConversationBusy`; an idle one rejects `whenIdle: "reject"` input with `ConversationIdle`. An idle continue places
queued items and starts a run with them and itself, placing no entry of its own. An idle conversation with queued
items queues it behind them and runs a final boundary. Otherwise idle input places its entry (`pi.user`, or the
input's own) and starts a run, and an idle write appends its entry and settles `done`, or `stale` when its head
reaches before the active range.

symbols.name: ConversationTranscript
symbols.comment:
What a client has of one conversation: every entry it got from a view or fetched, and the gaps between (spec §9.3).
A layer over any `ConversationView`, wherever it comes from: call `merge()` with every value of the view; it returns
the view with the client's whole transcript as `items` instead of the window. Entries never change once committed,
so the transcript only grows; a window that dropped its oldest entries keeps them here.

A window whose `before` lies past the newest entry the client has does not continue it, after a stall, an overflow,
or a reconnect: the entries in between become a gap. Nothing counts entries or computes ranges from entry IDs, which
have holes; only exclusive bounds are turned into the inclusive bounds of `EntryQuery`. After a drop, a new watch
with `resume` as its window continues the transcript.

A merge costs O(items) and never re-sorts or re-fetches; a merge, `loadEarlier()`, or `fillGap()` that adds nothing
returns the previous `items` array. Concurrent calls of `loadEarlier()`, or of `fillGap()` for the same gap, share one
load, so a placeholder that stays visible does not fetch twice.

see `call.parent`), applies output limits and the tool's replay policy, and reports progress in `pi.live.nestedTools`.

or is aborted returns an `isError` result.

The nested call's key names it within this call; its call ID is `<callId>/<key>`. By default the key is the call's
position among this invocation's nested calls, `1`, `2`, ... An explicit `key` must be non-empty, without `/`, not

`unanswered` with `turn_limit`. An integer, `1` or more; unset, no limit. Task-owned children and forks inherit it.

override. Task-owned children and forks inherit it.

Runs inside the creating commit, after the creation hook and the `agent` change. The conversation creation is already

symbols.name: CompactionPolicy
symbols.comment: Automatic compaction thresholds (spec §8.7); manual compaction ignores `enabled`.

symbols.name: enabled
symbols.comment: Threshold and overflow compaction.

symbols.name: reserveTokens
symbols.comment: Room kept free for the answer: generation blocks to compact above `contextWindow - reserveTokens`.

symbols.name: keepRecentTokens
symbols.comment: Approximate size of the recent context a summary keeps verbatim.

symbols.name: backgroundTokens
symbols.comment: Background compaction starts `backgroundTokens` below the blocking threshold; `0` disables it.

symbols.name: CompactionSettings
symbols.comment:
Compaction settings of the harness (`HarnessSettings.compaction`) or of one conversation (`AgentState.compaction`).
`modelOverrides` is keyed by exact `"provider/modelId"`; each field it sets replaces the general one for that model,
so small- and large-window models can share a harness.

symbols.name: ProgressPolicy
symbols.comment:
How often running progress is committed, and how long it may wait in memory before it is stored. Progress commits are
deferred (`CommitPersistence`): watches see each at once, and Storage gets them together, at the run's next phase
boundary or after `persistWithinMs`. A host can commit less often, so live answers and tool output appear in larger steps.

symbols.name: partialIntervalMs
symbols.comment: Minimum pause between commits of the answer being generated.

symbols.name: outputIntervalMs
symbols.comment: Minimum pause between commits of running tool output; large commits also pause in proportion to their size.

symbols.name: persistWithinMs
CompactionReason
symbols.comment: Why a compaction runs: `compact()`, a threshold in generation preparation, or a context overflow.

symbols.name: CompactionResult
symbols.signature: export type CompactionResult = { entryId?: EntryId; submissionId?: SubmissionId };
symbols.comment:
`entryId` of a blocking compaction's summary, or the `submissionId` of a conversation-owned compaction's summary
write; both absent when nothing was compacted.

symbols.name: HarnessSettings
symbols.comment: Harness-wide run policy. Read at every resolution and never copied; getters are fine. Synchronous: some readers run on the Session line.

symbols.name: extensions
symbols.comment: Default extension selection; absent: every installed extension, in install order.

symbols.name: contextRetentionMs
symbols.comment:
How long an idle conversation keeps its last context read in memory, so its next run reads only newer entries.
Busy conversations always keep it; `0` drops it once the conversation is idle.

symbols.name: documentRetentionMs
afterFailedRun
symbols.comment:
What a run that fails (`model_error`, `no_model`, `interrupted`, `restart_limit`, `nothing_to_answer`,
`turn_limit`) does with the inputs queued behind it: `keep` leaves them queued until the next input or queued write, `continue` starts the
next run with them, as an answer would, and `withdraw` settles them `unanswered` with reason `run_failed`. Default
`keep`.

symbols.name: restartLimit
symbols.comment:
How many times in a row a task may be cut off by a crash, eviction, or reset (a close does not count) without
changing its state before it ends instead of running again: a tool call with an error result, a compaction failed
into `pi.live.compactionFailure`, a run with `pi.live.runFailure` reason `restart_limit`, any other task `faulted`
with detail `{ reason: "restart_limit" }`. A generation's request or poll the host died during is a failed attempt
under `retry` first; the limit bounds it only when charging that attempt keeps being cut off. Default 5;
`Infinity` never ends a task for it.

symbols.name: AfterFailedRun
symbols.comment:
What a failed run does with the inputs queued behind it (`HarnessSettings.afterFailedRun`): a run that ends with
`model_error`, `no_model`, `interrupted`, `restart_limit`, `nothing_to_answer`, or `turn_limit`.

symbols.name: extensions

symbols.name: compaction
symbols.comment: Harness-wide policy over the defaults; per-model overrides apply where the model is known.

symbols.name: HarnessOptions
telemetry
